blocks.x: An inequality says one quantity is larger than another rather than equal to it. Nearly every move chapter 4 used on equations, adding the same number to both sides or scaling both sides, carries over unchanged. Exactly one does not, and finding which one, and why it fails, is the work of this lesson.

Three warehouses each store a whole number of pallets. Warehouse A stores more than warehouse B, and warehouse B stores more than warehouse C. Warehouse C stores \(47\) pallets. Enter the smallest number of pallets warehouse A could store.
hints: Comparing \(A\) with \(C\) in one step gives a true statement, but a weaker one than the two given comparisons allow. Work out what \(B\) must be first.
\(B\) is a whole number above \(47\), so the smallest \(B\) can be is \(48\). Now take the same step one more time, from \(B\) to \(A\).
blocks.sol: Since \(B>47\) and \(B\) is a whole number, \(B\) is at least \(48\), and since \(A>B\), \(A\) is at least \(49\). The triple \(49,48,47\) satisfies every condition, so the smallest count is \(\boxed{49}\). Comparing \(A\) with \(C\) directly gives the weaker \(A>47\), which is true but allows \(A=48\), a value the step through \(B\) rules out.

blocks.x: At the start of a shift the first bin holds \(415\) bolts and the second holds \(392\). A machine then drops \(168\) bolts into each bin. Enter how many more bolts the first bin holds than the second after the drop.
hints: Ask what happens to the gap between the two bins, not to either count on its own.
The two counts become \(415+168\) and \(392+168\). Subtract one from the other.
blocks.sol: After the drop the counts are \(415+168=583\) and \(392+168=560\), and \(583-560=\boxed{23}\), the same gap as \(415-392\) before it. Both counts go up by the same \(168\), so the gap is untouched. Adding \(168\) to the gap instead gives \(191\), which would be right only if the bolts all went into the first bin.

blocks.x: The statement \(a\gt b\) means that \(a-b\) is positive, and \(a\ge b\) means that \(a-b\) is positive or zero. Every rule in this chapter comes from reading a comparison that way. Transitivity. If \(a\gt b\) and \(b\gt c\), then \(a-b\) and \(b-c\) are both positive, so their sum \((a-b)+(b-c)=a-c\) is positive as well, and \(a\gt c\). Adding or subtracting the same number on both sides leaves the direction alone, since \((a+c)-(b+c)=a-b\) is the difference it was before, which is why adding \(168\) bolts to each bin left the gap at \(23\).

A hiking club logged two trips. The first covered more than \(34\) kilometers and the second covered more than \(57\) kilometers, and neither distance has to be a whole number. Enter the largest number of kilometers that the two trips together are guaranteed to exceed.
hints: Each trip has its own number to beat. The two comparisons point the same way, so they can be combined into one comparison about the total.
Write each trip as a comparison, then add the two left sides together and the two right sides together. Test the result on a sample pair such as \(34.2\) and \(57.3\).
blocks.sol: The first distance is more than \(34\) and the second is more than \(57\), and two comparisons pointing the same way may be added, so the total is more than \(34+57=\boxed{91}\). Writing the two distances as \(f\) and \(s\), both \(f-34\) and \(s-57\) are positive, so \((f+s)-91\) is positive as well. Distances just above \(34\) and \(57\) give a total just above \(91\), so no larger number works.

blocks.x: A swim club beat a tennis club in wins two years running, \(41\) to \(12\) in the first year and \(44\) to \(39\) in the second. Subtracting the first comparison from the second, the way two equations are subtracted, gives the conclusion that the swim club's gain in wins was the larger one. Enter how many more wins the tennis club gained from the first year to the second than the swim club gained.
hints: Both stated comparisons are true, so if subtracting one from the other were a legal move, its conclusion would have to be true as well. Work out each club's gain on its own.
The swim club went from \(41\) to \(44\) and the tennis club went from \(12\) to \(39\). Subtract within each club, then compare the two gains.
blocks.sol: The swim club gained \(44-41=3\) wins and the tennis club gained \(39-12=27\), so the tennis club's gain is larger by \(27-3=\boxed{24}\). The subtraction gives \(3>27\), which is false even though both starting comparisons are true, so one inequality may not be subtracted from another.

blocks.x: Two inequalities pointing the same way may be added. If \(x\gt y\) and \(a\gt b\), then \(x-y\) and \(a-b\) are both positive, so their sum \((x+a)-(y+b)\) is positive and \(x+a\gt y+b\). They may not be subtracted. Subtracting them would need \((x-a)-(y-b)=(x-y)-(a-b)\) to be positive, and one positive number minus another is positive, zero or negative depending on which of the two is larger. With the swim club's gain of \(3\) and the tennis club's \(27\), that difference is negative and the claim \(3\gt 27\) is false.

blocks.cap: Two numbers sit to the right of zero with \(a\) nearer to it, so \(a\lt b\). Multiplying both by the same negative number sends each to the other side of zero, and they cross on the way, so the image of \(a\) finishes to the RIGHT of the image of \(b\). The crossing is the whole rule: the direction of the comparison reverses.

blocks.x: Adding shifts both sides by the same amount and leaves the difference alone. Multiplying does not, since \(cx-cy=c(x-y)\) scales that difference by \(c\). Scaling a positive number by a positive \(c\) keeps it positive, and scaling by a negative \(c\) makes it negative, so multiplying splits into two cases. The next two problems take one of each.

A press stamped \(t\) parts on Monday, with \(t>185\). On Tuesday it stamped \(3\) times Monday's number and then \(40\) more. Apply those same two operations to both sides of \(t>185\). The result says Tuesday's count is greater than a certain number. Enter that number.
hints: Tuesday's count is \(3t+40\). Build it up from \(t\gt 185\) one operation at a time.
Multiplying both sides by \(3\) is multiplying by a positive number, so the direction holds. Now add \(40\) to both sides.
blocks.sol: Multiplying \(t>185\) by the positive number \(3\) keeps the direction, giving \(3t>555\), and adding \(40\) to both sides keeps it as well, so Tuesday's count satisfies \(3t+40>\boxed{595}\). The direction holds through both steps because \(3\) is positive and adding \(40\) changes both sides by the same amount.

blocks.x: A student divides both sides of \(-7x>91\) by \(-7\), leaves the inequality symbol pointing the same way, and concludes that the smallest integer \(x\) can be is \(-12\). Enter the largest integer \(x\) can actually be.
hints: Test the student's answer against the original statement before doing anything else. Put \(x=-12\) into \(-7x\) and compare the result with \(91\).
Dividing both sides by \(-7\) reverses the direction, so the allowed values sit below \(-13\) rather than above it.
blocks.sol: Dividing \(-7x\gt 91\) by \(-7\) reverses the direction to \(x\lt -13\), so the largest integer available is \(\boxed{-14}\). Checking, \(-7(-14)=98\gt 91\) while \(-7(-13)=91\) is not above \(91\). The student's \(-12\) fails outright, since \(-7(-12)=84\) sits below \(91\).

blocks.x: Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the direction. Start from \(x\gt y\), so \(x-y\) is positive. For a negative \(c\), the product \(c(x-y)\) is a negative times a positive and so is negative, and since \(c(x-y)=cx-cy\), that makes \(cx-cy\) negative and \(cx\lt cy\). For a positive \(c\) the same product stays positive, so \(cx\gt cy\) and the direction holds. Dividing by \(c\) is multiplying by \(\frac{1}{c}\), which has the same sign as \(c\), so division splits the same two ways. Skipping that reversal in \(-7x\gt 91\) produced the wrong \(-12\).

Choosing between those two cases takes the sign of the multiplier. With a number written out the sign is there to read. With a letter it is not, and there are three cases rather than two, since multiplying by zero gives \(0\) on both sides. The next problem asks what that leaves.
It is given that \(a>b\), and \(k\) is a real number whose sign is not stated. Enter one word, greater, less, equal or unknown, for how \(ka\) compares with \(kb\).
hints: Write \(ka-kb=k(a-b)\). Since \(a-b\) is positive, the sign of \(ka-kb\) matches the sign of \(k\).
Fix \(a=9\) and \(b=2\), then try \(k=4\), \(k=-4\) and \(k=0\) in turn, comparing \(ka\) with \(kb\) each time.
blocks.sol: Here \(ka-kb=k(a-b)\) and \(a-b\) is positive, so the sign of that difference is the sign of \(k\). With \(a=9\) and \(b=2\), \(k=4\) gives \(36\gt 8\), \(k=-4\) gives \(-36\lt -8\), and \(k=0\) gives \(0=0\), so the comparison is \(\boxed{\text{unknown}}\). All three cases are possible, so an inequality cannot be multiplied by a letter whose sign is not known.

blocks.x: Thomas Harriot wrote the signs \(\lt \) and \(\gt \) in his own papers and published none of his mathematics. Both first appeared in print in 1631, ten years after he died, in a book other hands assembled from those papers.

It is given that \(m>n\), with nothing said about the signs of \(m\) and \(n\), and \(t\) is a real number. Statement 1 is \(m-9>n-9\). Statement 2 is \(-2m>-2n\). Statement 3 is \(\frac{m}{5}>\frac{n}{5}\). Statement 4 is \(mt>nt\). Statement 5 is \(m+n>2n\). Statement 6 is \(m-n>0\). Enter how many of the six must be true.
hints: Each statement is one move applied to both sides of \(m\gt n\). Name the move first, then ask whether that move preserves the direction.
Statement 5 is \(m\gt n\) with \(n\) added to both sides, and statement 6 is what \(m\gt n\) means written out. Check the other four against what each operation does to the direction.
blocks.sol: Statement 1 subtracts \(9\) from both sides, statement 3 divides by the positive number \(5\), statement 5 adds \(n\) to both sides, and statement 6 restates \(m>n\), so those four hold. Statement 2 multiplies by \(-2\) without reversing the direction and statement 4 multiplies by a letter whose sign is not stated, so the count is \(\boxed{4}\). The signs of \(m\) and \(n\) never matter here. Only the sign of each multiplier does.

blocks.x: Multiply or divide both sides by a letter only when you know the sign of that letter. With \(m\gt n\), the comparison between \(km\) and \(kn\) is decided by the sign of \(km-kn=k(m-n)\), and since \(m-n\) is positive that sign is the sign of \(k\). If \(k\) is positive then \(km\gt kn\), if \(k\) is negative then \(km\lt kn\), and if \(k=0\) then \(km=kn\). Three cases and three different outcomes, so nothing is settled until the sign is known, which is why \(mt\gt nt\) stayed out of the count. Dividing by a letter needs the same condition and also \(k \neq 0\).

A square is never negative, whatever real number is put into it. Squaring means multiplying a number by itself, so the two factors are the same number and have the same sign. A positive times a positive is positive, a negative times a negative is positive, and \(0\times 0\) is \(0\). So \(x^2\) is never negative, whatever real \(x\) is.
For every real number \(x\), the quantity \(x^2+82-18x\) is equal to \((x-9)^2+1\). How does \(x^2+82\) compare with \(18x\) at every real \(x\)? Enter one word, greater, less, equal or unknown.
hints: Deciding which is larger is the same as deciding the sign of the difference \(x^2+82-18x\), and the problem already gives that difference in a second form.
\((x-9)^2\) is the square of a real number, so it is never negative. Add \(1\) and ask how small the whole thing can get.
blocks.sol: The difference \(x^2+82-18x\) equals \((x-9)^2+1\), and the square of a real number is never negative, so that difference is at least \(1\) at every real \(x\). Since the difference is always positive, \(x^2+82\) is \(\boxed{\text{greater}}\). Rearranging the two quantities is not enough on its own. You need \(x^2\ge 0\), applied to \(x-9\).

blocks.x: Each of these four pairs has \(x\gt y\). Pair 1 is \(x=9\), \(y=4\). Pair 2 is \(x=-2\), \(y=-5\). Pair 3 is \(x=7\), \(y=-1\). Pair 4 is \(x=-4\), \(y=-8\). Enter how many of the four pairs satisfy \(\frac{1}{x}\lt \frac{1}{y}\).
hints: Work out both reciprocals in each pair and compare them. A negative number has a negative reciprocal, and of two negative numbers the one further from zero is the smaller.
Watch for the pair where \(x\) is positive and \(y\) is negative. There \(\frac{1}{x}\) is positive while \(\frac{1}{y}\) is negative, and no positive number is less than a negative one.
blocks.sol: Pair 1 gives \(\frac{1}{9}\lt \frac{1}{4}\), pair 2 gives \(-\frac{1}{2}\lt -\frac{1}{5}\) and pair 4 gives \(-\frac{1}{4}\lt -\frac{1}{8}\), while pair 3 gives \(\frac{1}{7}\gt -1\), so the count is \(\boxed{3}\). The three that flip have \(x\) and \(y\) on the same side of zero, and pair 3 does not.

blocks.x: The trivial inequality. \(x^2\ge 0\) for every real \(x\), with equality only at \(x=0\), since a nonzero \(x\) times itself is a positive times a positive or a negative times a negative, and either way the product is positive. The reciprocal rule. If \(x\gt y\) and \(x\) and \(y\) share a sign, then \(\frac{1}{x}\lt \frac{1}{y}\). Dividing \(x\gt y\) by \(xy\) gives \(\frac{1}{y}\gt \frac{1}{x}\), and \(xy\) is positive exactly because the two signs match. With \(x\) and \(y\) on opposite sides of zero \(xy\) is negative and that division reverses instead, which is pair 3 above.

Every rule in this lesson is one question about a sign. Adding or subtracting the same number never changes a direction. Multiplying or dividing changes it exactly when the multiplier is negative, and leaves it undetermined when the multiplier is a letter of unstated sign. The last two problems run several of these moves in one chain.
Two numbers satisfy \(p>11\) and \(q>-3\), and nothing else is known about either one. Enter the smallest number that \(4-6(p+q)\) must stay below.
hints: Two inequalities pointing the same way may be added, so pin down what \(p+q\) must exceed before touching anything else.
That gives \(p+q\gt 8\). Multiplying both sides by \(-6\) is multiplying by a negative, so settle the direction before adding \(4\).
blocks.sol: Adding \(p\gt 11\) and \(q\gt -3\) gives \(p+q\gt 8\), multiplying by \(-6\) reverses the direction to \(-6(p+q)\lt -48\), and adding \(4\) to both sides gives \(4-6(p+q)\lt \boxed{-44}\). Skipping the reversal would give \(4-6(p+q)\gt -44\), which is false at \(p=12\) and \(q=-2\), since those give \(-56\).

blocks.x: Two numbers satisfy \(15-8s>15-8t\), and their product \(st\) is positive. Neither one is known to be positive on its own. Enter one word, greater, less, equal or unknown, for how \(\frac{1}{t}\) compares with \(\frac{1}{s}\).
hints: Two moves. First turn \(15-8s\gt 15-8t\) into a comparison between \(s\) and \(t\) alone, watching the step that reverses the direction.
That gives \(s\lt t\). The reciprocal rule needs the two numbers to share a sign, and \(st\gt 0\) says exactly that even though neither sign is known on its own.
blocks.sol: Subtracting \(15\) from both sides gives \(-8s\gt -8t\), and dividing by \(-8\) reverses the direction to \(s\lt t\). Since \(st\gt 0\) the two share a sign, so the reciprocal rule applies and \(\frac{1}{t}\) compared with \(\frac{1}{s}\) is \(\boxed{\text{less}}\). Both sign cases check out, \(s=1,t=2\) giving \(\frac{1}{2}\lt 1\) and \(s=-2,t=-1\) giving \(-1\lt -\frac{1}{2}\). Drop \(st\gt 0\) and the answer is unknown, since \(s=-1,t=2\) gives \(\frac{1}{t}\gt \frac{1}{s}\).

blocks.x: Every rule here says what one move does to a comparison already in hand. Lesson 8.2, Which Is Bigger, uses them in the other direction. It starts with two specific quantities too awkward to compute outright and looks for the move that settles which one is larger.

review.x: \(w\) is an integer and \(w-18>45\). Enter the smallest value \(w\) can be.
hints: Adding \(18\) to both sides leaves the direction alone.
That gives \(w\gt 63\), and \(63\) itself does not satisfy \(w\gt 63\).
review.sol: Adding \(18\) to both sides leaves the direction unchanged, giving \(w>63\), so the smallest integer available is \(\boxed{64}\). Checking, \(64-18=46>45\) while \(63-18=45\) is not above \(45\).

review.x: Integers \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) satisfy \(a>b\) and \(b>c\), with \(c=61\). Enter the smallest possible value of \(a\).
hints: Comparing \(a\) with \(c\) directly gives only \(a\gt 61\), which leaves out the integer \(b\) strictly between them.
\(b\) is an integer above \(61\), so \(b\) is at least \(62\). Apply the same reasoning to \(a\).
review.sol: Since \(b\gt 61\) and \(b\) is an integer, \(b\) is at least \(62\), and \(a\gt b\) makes \(a\) at least \(63\). The triple \(63,62,61\) meets every condition, so the answer is \(\boxed{63}\). Chaining to \(a\gt 61\) first is true but weaker, since \(a=62\) would need an integer \(b\) with \(61\lt b\lt 62\), and there is none.

review.x: A number \(g\) satisfies \(g>16\). Enter the largest number that \(7g\) must exceed.
hints: Multiplying both sides of \(g\gt 16\) by \(7\) is multiplying by a positive number, so the direction of the inequality is unchanged.
The value you want is the boundary that \(7g\) stays above. Work out \(7g\) with \(g\) sitting right at \(16\), even though \(g\) never equals \(16\).
review.sol: Multiplying \(g>16\) by the positive number \(7\) leaves the direction unchanged, so \(7g>\boxed{112}\). Nothing larger works, since \(g\) can sit just above \(16\), which puts \(7g\) just above \(112\).

review.x: Real numbers \(m\) and \(n\) satisfy \(m>30\) and \(n>17\). Enter the largest number that \(m+n\) must exceed.
hints: The two inequalities point the same way, so they can be combined into one.
Add the two left sides together and the two right sides together, then read off the number on the right.
review.sol: Two inequalities pointing the same way may be added, so \(m+n>30+17=\boxed{47}\). Nothing larger works, since taking \(m\) and \(n\) just above \(30\) and \(17\) makes \(m+n\) as close to \(47\) as we like.

review.x: \(q\) is an integer and \(\frac{q}{8}>13\). Enter the smallest value \(q\) can be.
hints: Multiplying both sides by \(8\) is multiplying by a positive number, so the direction holds.
That gives \(q\gt 104\), and \(104\) itself is not above \(104\).
review.sol: Multiplying both sides by the positive number \(8\) keeps the direction, giving \(q>104\), so the smallest integer is \(\boxed{105}\). Checking, \(\frac{105}{8}=13.125\) is above \(13\) while \(\frac{104}{8}=13\) is not.

review.x: A number \(k\) satisfies \(k>3\), and nothing else is known about it. Enter the smallest number that \(-8k\) must stay below.
hints: Multiplying both sides by \(-8\) is multiplying by a negative, so settle the direction of the comparison before settling the number.
The number on the other side comes from applying that same multiplication to the boundary \(3\). Then test \(k=4\) to check the direction you chose.
review.sol: Multiplying \(k\gt 3\) by \(-8\) reverses the direction, so \(-8k\lt \boxed{-24}\). Keeping \(\gt \) would give the false claim \(-8k\gt -24\), since \(k=4\) gives \(-32\), and \(-32\) is not above \(-24\).

review.x: \(n\) is an integer and \(-5n>37\). Enter the largest value \(n\) can be.
hints: Dividing both sides of \(-5n\gt 37\) by \(-5\) reverses the direction of the inequality.
That gives \(n\lt -7.4\), so find the largest integer that is strictly below \(-7.4\).
review.sol: Dividing \(-5n\gt 37\) by \(-5\) reverses the direction to \(n\lt -7.4\), so the largest integer is \(\boxed{-8}\). Checking, \(-5(-8)=40\gt 37\) while \(-5(-7)=35\) is not above \(37\).

review.x: Both \(20>3\) and \(b>1\) are true, and \(b\) is an integer. Subtracting the second comparison from the first would claim \(20-b>3-1\). Enter the smallest integer \(b\) that makes that claim false.
hints: Work out the right side first, then watch the left side shrink as \(b\) grows.
At \(b=14\) the claim reads \(6\gt 2\) and holds. Step \(b\) up one at a time until the left side is no longer bigger than \(2\).
review.sol: The claim reads \(20-b\gt 2\), which holds only while \(b\lt 18\). At \(b=18\) it reads \(2\gt 2\), which is false, so the answer is \(\boxed{18}\). Both starting comparisons still hold at \(b=18\), so subtracting one comparison from another is not a legal move.

review.x: It is given that \(a>b\), and \(t=0\). Enter one word, greater, less, equal or unknown, for how \(ta\) compares with \(tb\).
hints: The rules for multiplying both sides cover a positive multiplier and a negative multiplier. Zero is neither of those, so neither rule settles this one.
Work out \(ta\) and \(tb\) directly rather than reasoning about direction.
review.sol: With \(t=0\), both \(ta\) and \(tb\) are \(0\), so the two are \(\boxed{\text{equal}}\). Zero is neither positive nor negative, so neither multiplication rule applies, and the given \(a>b\) makes no difference to the comparison.

review.x: It is given that \(u\gt v\). Statement 1 is \(u+3\gt v+3\). Statement 2 is \(4u\gt 4v\). Statement 3 is \(\frac{u}{-2}\gt \frac{v}{-2}\). Statement 4 is \(u-v\gt 0\). Statement 5 is \(-u\lt -v\). Statement 6 is \(u+v\gt 2v\). Enter how many of the six must be true.
hints: Each statement is the result of one move applied to both sides of \(u\gt v\). Name the move first, then ask whether that move leaves the direction alone.

Adding or subtracting the same quantity, and multiplying or dividing by a positive, all leave the direction alone. Multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses it, so check the direction carefully on every statement that carries a negative.
review.sol: Dividing both sides by \(-2\) reverses the direction, so statement 3 is the only one that fails and the count is \(\boxed{5}\). Statements 1, 4 and 6 come from adding or subtracting the same quantity on both sides, statement 2 from multiplying by the positive \(4\), and statement 5 from multiplying by \(-1\) with the direction reversed.

review.x: It is given that \(x>y\). For how many of \(k=-3\), \(k=0\) and \(k=5\) is \(kx>ky\) guaranteed? Enter that count.
hints: Compare the two sides through \(kx-ky=k(x-y)\), and note that \(x-y\) is positive.
Multiplying by a negative reverses the direction, and \(k=0\) needs a separate check since both sides become \(0\).
review.sol: The sign of \(kx-ky=k(x-y)\) is the sign of \(k\), since \(x-y\) is positive. So \(k=5\) gives \(kx\gt ky\), \(k=-3\) gives \(kx\lt ky\), and \(k=0\) gives \(kx=ky\), leaving \(\boxed{1}\). Three values of \(k\) and three different outcomes, so you may only multiply both sides by a letter when you know its sign.

review.x: A real number \(c\) satisfies \(c^2\le 0\). Enter the value of \((c+5)(c+8)\).
hints: A square is never negative for a real number, so ask which values make \(c^2\le 0\) possible at all.
The only real \(c\) with \(c^2\le 0\) is \(c=0\). Substitute it into both factors.
review.sol: Since \(c^2\ge 0\) for every real \(c\), the condition \(c^2\le 0\) can hold only when \(c^2=0\), so \(c=0\) and \((0+5)(0+8)=\boxed{40}\). The trivial inequality pins \(c\) to a single value, so nothing else about \(c\) has to be found.

review.x: For every real number \(x\), the quantity \(x^2+121-22x\) is equal to \((x-11)^2\). Enter the value of \(x^2+121\) at the one real number \(x\) where it equals \(22x\).
hints: A square of a real number is never negative, and it is zero only when the thing being squared is zero.
review.sol: \(x^2+121\) equals \(22x\) exactly when \(x^2+121-22x=0\), which is \((x-11)^2=0\), so \(x=11\). Then \(x^2+121=121+121=\boxed{242}\), and \(22(11)=242\) agrees. A square is never negative, so \((x-11)^2\) is \(0\) at one value of \(x\) and positive everywhere else, which is why \(x^2+121\) is never below \(22x\).

review.x: The numbers \(x=15\) and \(y=6\) are both positive, and \(x>y\). Enter the value of \(\frac{1}{y}-\frac{1}{x}\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Use \(30\) as the common denominator, since it is the smallest number both \(6\) and \(15\) divide.
That gives \(\frac{5}{30}-\frac{2}{30}\). Reduce the result.
review.sol: With a common denominator of \(30\), \(\frac{1}{6}-\frac{1}{15}=\frac{5}{30}-\frac{2}{30}=\frac{3}{30}=\boxed{\frac{1}{10}}\). The reciprocal rule says that when \(x\gt y\) and both are positive, \(\frac{1}{x}\lt \frac{1}{y}\), so this difference had to come out positive.

review.x: The numbers \(x=10\) and \(y=-4\) satisfy \(x\gt y\), so the reciprocal rule would claim \(\frac{1}{x}\lt \frac{1}{y}\). Enter the value of \(\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{y}\) as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Work out both reciprocals first, keeping the sign of \(\frac{1}{-4}\).
Subtracting a negative adds, so the computation is \(\frac{1}{10}+\frac{1}{4}\) with a common denominator of \(20\).
review.sol: The reciprocals are \(\frac{1}{10}\) and \(-\frac{1}{4}\), so \(\frac{1}{10}-\left(-\frac{1}{4}\right)=\frac{2}{20}+\frac{5}{20}=\boxed{\frac{7}{20}}\). The difference is positive, which says \(\frac{1}{x}>\frac{1}{y}\), the opposite of the claim. These two numbers sit on opposite sides of zero, and the rule needs them on the same side.

review.x: A number \(z\) satisfies \(z\lt 6\), and \(y=9-4z\). Enter the largest number that \(y\) must exceed.
hints: Multiply both sides of \(z\lt 6\) by \(-4\) first, and remember that multiplying by a negative reverses the direction.
That gives \(-4z\gt -24\). Now add \(9\) to both sides, which leaves the direction alone.
review.sol: Multiplying \(z\lt 6\) by \(-4\) reverses the direction to \(-4z\gt -24\), and adding \(9\) to both sides gives \(9-4z\gt \boxed{-15}\). Skipping the reversal gives \(y\lt -15\) instead, which is false at \(z=0\), where \(y=9\).

review.x: An integer \(m\) satisfies \(\frac{1}{m}\lt \frac{1}{7}\) and \(m\gt 0\). Enter the smallest value \(m\) can be.
hints: Both \(m\) and \(7\) are positive, so the same-sign condition is met and taking reciprocals reverses the comparison.
The reversal turns \(\frac{1}{m}\lt \frac{1}{7}\) into \(m\gt 7\), and that comparison is strict, so \(m=7\) is ruled out.
review.sol: Both numbers are positive, so taking reciprocals reverses the comparison and \(\frac{1}{m}\lt \frac{1}{7}\) becomes \(m\gt 7\), making the smallest integer \(\boxed{8}\). Checking, \(\frac{1}{8}\lt \frac{1}{7}\). The condition \(m\gt 0\) matters, since \(m=-3\) also satisfies \(\frac{1}{m}\lt \frac{1}{7}\) but is not greater than \(7\).

blocks.x: Every problem in this lesson gives two quantities and asks which one is larger. The rules from 8.1 are the tools, and the work is choosing which one to reach for. Several of these pairs are built so computing both is slow, and one is out of reach by hand, so the route has to settle the comparison without producing either value.
Two sums are \(A=\frac{5}{8}+\frac{7}{9}\) and \(B=\frac{5}{9}+\frac{7}{8}\). Do not compute either sum. Work out \(A-B\) instead and read its sign. Enter \(A\) or \(B\), whichever is bigger.
hints: Write \(A-B\) as one string of four fractions, then group the two with denominator \(8\) and the two with denominator \(9\) before anything else.
Grouping the eighths gives \(\frac{5}{8}-\frac{7}{8}=-\frac{1}{4}\) and grouping the ninths gives \(\frac{7}{9}-\frac{5}{9}=\frac{2}{9}\). Add those two results and read the sign.
blocks.sol: Group the eighths and the ninths. \(A-B=\left(\frac{5}{8}-\frac{7}{8}\right)+\left(\frac{7}{9}-\frac{5}{9}\right)=-\frac{1}{4}+\frac{2}{9}=-\frac{9}{36}+\frac{8}{36}=-\frac{1}{36}\), which is negative, so the bigger sum is \(\boxed{B}\). Both sums are built from the numerators \(5\) and \(7\) over the denominators \(8\) and \(9\) with the pairing swapped, so they differ by only \(\frac{1}{36}\).

blocks.x: Let \(A=987654\times 987656\) and \(B=987655^2\). Both are twelve-digit numbers, so multiplying them out by hand is not the route. Enter the value of \(B-A\).
hints: There is no need to compute either number. Rewrite \(987656\) as \(987655+1\) and distribute, so that \(A\) becomes \(987654\times 987655\) plus a leftover.
Split \(B=987655\times 987655\) the same way, writing one factor as \(987654+1\). Both quantities then contain \(987654\times 987655\), and only the leftovers differ.
blocks.sol: Since \(987656=987655+1\), distributing gives \(A=987654\times 987655+987654\), and writing \(B=(987654+1)\times 987655\) gives \(B=987654\times 987655+987655\). The first piece is the same in both, so \(B-A=987655-987654=\boxed{1}\). Splitting each quantity so that a common piece appears turns a twelve-digit subtraction into a one-digit one.

blocks.x: Comparing two numbers is deciding the sign of their difference. From 8.1, \(a\gt b\) means \(a-b\) is positive, \(a\lt b\) means \(a-b\) is negative, and \(a=b\) means \(a-b\) is zero. So two numbers to evaluate turn into one expression whose sign has to be found. Whatever the two have in common cancels in the subtraction and never has to be worked out, so \(A-B\) can be short even when \(A\) and \(B\) are both long.
Let \(A=\frac{12}{49}\) and \(B=\frac{8}{33}\). The denominators share no factor, so a common denominator would be a large one. Enter A or B, whichever is bigger.
hints: \(12\) and \(8\) both divide \(24\), so both fractions can be written with the same numerator.
Multiply \(A\) top and bottom by \(2\) and \(B\) top and bottom by \(3\). Then only the denominators differ.
blocks.sol: Rewrite both with numerator \(24\). Then \(A=\frac{24}{98}\) and \(B=\frac{24}{99}\), and \(98\lt 99\), so the bigger one is \(\boxed{A}\). Cutting the same \(24\) into \(98\) pieces gives bigger pieces than cutting it into \(99\), so the larger denominator gives the smaller number.

blocks.x: Let \(A=9^{15}\) and \(B=27^{10}\). Working out either power is a long job, and neither one has to be done. Enter A or B, whichever is bigger, or the word equal if neither is.
hints: \(9=3^2\) and \(27=3^3\), so both can be written as powers of \(3\).
Raising a power to a power multiplies the exponents, the rule from 3.1. Get both exponents, then compare them.
blocks.sol: Both bases are powers of \(3\). Then \(A=(3^2)^{15}=3^{30}\) and \(B=(3^3)^{10}=3^{30}\), so the answer is \(\boxed{\text{equal}}\). \(B\) has the bigger base and \(A\) the bigger exponent, so neither one of those settles it. Written with base \(3\), only the exponents are left to compare, and they match.

blocks.x: Rewriting both numbers into the same form leaves one part to compare. For two fractions with the same numerator, the bigger one is the one with the smaller denominator, since cutting a fixed positive amount into more pieces makes each piece smaller, so \(\frac{c}{p}\gt \frac{c}{q}\) exactly when \(p\lt q\), for positive \(c\), \(p\) and \(q\). The same holds for powers once both are written on one base, since comparing \(3^{m}\) with \(3^{n}\) is comparing \(m\) with \(n\) and nothing else. When no common base is available, write both with a common exponent instead.

blocks.cap: The two brackets are the only comparisons made. Each one is a single comparison between \(m\) and an outer point, and the two together are enough for \(a\lt b\), with no direct comparison between \(a\) and \(b\) anywhere. Choosing \(m\) is the work, since it has to sit above one and below the other.

blocks.x: Neither number of a pair has to be measured against the other directly. Transitivity from 8.1 says that if \(a\lt m\) and \(m\lt b\) then \(a\lt b\), so choosing one number in the middle replaces a single hard comparison with two easy ones.
Let \(A=\frac{138}{137}\) and \(B=\frac{265}{266}\). A common denominator here is \(36442\). Enter A or B, whichever is bigger.
hints: Building that common denominator is the long way round. Look instead for one simple number that separates the two.
A positive fraction sits above \(1\) when its numerator is the larger of the two numbers, and below \(1\) when its denominator is. Check \(138\) against \(137\), then \(265\) against \(266\).
blocks.sol: Compare each with \(1\). The fraction \(\frac{138}{137}\) has the larger number on top, so it sits above \(1\), and \(\frac{265}{266}\) has the larger number underneath, so it sits below \(1\). That gives \(A\gt 1\gt B\), and the bigger one is \(\boxed{A}\). The common denominator \(36442\) never had to be built.

blocks.x: Let \(A=\frac{17}{40}\) and \(B=\frac{22}{51}\). Both sit below \(\frac{1}{2}\) and above \(\frac{2}{5}\), so neither of those settles the pair. Enter A or B, whichever is bigger, or the word equal if neither is.
hints: A middle number settles the pair only when the two land on opposite sides of it, so the one you want is a fraction strictly inside the gap the statement names.
Sevenths land in that gap, since \(\frac{2}{5}\lt \frac{3}{7}\lt \frac{1}{2}\). Compare each of the two with \(\frac{3}{7}\) by cross-multiplying.
blocks.sol: Try sevenths. Since \(17\times 7=119\) and \(3\times 40=120\), \(A\lt \frac{3}{7}\), and since \(22\times 7=154\) and \(3\times 51=153\), \(B\gt \frac{3}{7}\). So \(A\lt \frac{3}{7}\lt B\) and the bigger one is \(\boxed{B}\). Halves and fifths fail here because they leave both numbers on the same side.

blocks.x: A middle number is useful only when the two numbers sit on opposite sides of it. The chain \(a\lt m\lt b\) needs one number below \(m\) and one above, so if both come out above \(m\), or both below it, that choice settles nothing and another one is needed. The work is choosing \(m\), and the usual choices are a round number such as \(1\) or a power of ten, or a simple fraction such as \(\frac{1}{2}\) sitting between the two.

Two numbers with awkward digits can have reciprocals that are easy to read. The bigger of two numbers of the same sign has the smaller reciprocal, so comparing the reciprocals settles the original pair, with the result read backwards.
Let \(A=\frac{31}{218}\) and \(B=\frac{23}{162}\). Enter \(A\) or \(B\), whichever is bigger.
hints: Computing both decimals is the slow route here. Both numbers are positive, so both can be flipped, and of two positive numbers the bigger one has the smaller reciprocal.
Divide \(218\) by \(31\), then \(162\) by \(23\). Each division has remainder \(1\), so each reciprocal is \(7\) plus a unit fraction.
blocks.sol: Both are positive, so flip both. \(\frac{1}{A}=\frac{218}{31}=7+\frac{1}{31}\) and \(\frac{1}{B}=\frac{162}{23}=7+\frac{1}{23}\). Since \(\frac{1}{31}\lt \frac{1}{23}\), \(\frac{1}{A}\lt \frac{1}{B}\), so the bigger number is \(\boxed{A}\). Flipping replaced a hard pair with an easy one, but the comparison reverses, since of two positive numbers the bigger one has the smaller reciprocal.

blocks.x: Pierre Bouguer printed the first \(\le\) and \(\ge\) in 1734, about a century after \(\lt\) and \(\gt\) first appeared in print. The bar he put under each sign covers the case where the two sides are equal.
Two numbers \(A\) and \(B\) satisfy \(\frac{1}{A}=\frac{4}{9}-\frac{7}{12}\) and \(\frac{1}{B}=\frac{5}{6}-\frac{3}{8}\). Enter the letter of the bigger number, \(A\) or \(B\).
hints: Work out \(\frac{1}{A}\) and \(\frac{1}{B}\) as single fractions first, then look at the sign of each.
One of the two reciprocals is negative, so the reciprocal rule does not apply here. A number and its reciprocal always have the same sign.
blocks.sol: \(\frac{1}{A}=\frac{16}{36}-\frac{21}{36}=-\frac{5}{36}\) and \(\frac{1}{B}=\frac{20}{24}-\frac{9}{24}=\frac{11}{24}\), so \(A\) is negative and \(B\) is positive, which makes the bigger number \(\boxed{B}\). The reciprocal rule only applies when both numbers are on the same side of zero. Without that check, \(\frac{1}{A}\lt \frac{1}{B}\) would be reversed into the false claim \(A\gt B\).

blocks.x: For two numbers of the same sign, the bigger one has the smaller reciprocal. That is 8.1's reciprocal rule, and using it as a tactic means comparing \(\frac{1}{A}\) with \(\frac{1}{B}\) and then reading the result backwards. The shared sign is the condition, and it is not a formality. If \(A\) and \(B\) sit on opposite sides of zero, their reciprocals sit on those same sides, no reversal applies, and the positive number is the bigger one whatever the two reciprocals are. Check the signs before flipping.

A second way to find the answer is to assume it. Suppose one of the two is bigger, then apply the same move to both sides until the statement is plainly true or plainly false. A false ending means the other one is bigger. That finds the answer, and whether it also proves it is a separate question.

Let \(A=-\left(\sqrt{5}+\sqrt{11}\right)\) and \(B=-\left(\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{14}\right)\). Assume one is bigger, square both sides, and check whether that step can be run backwards. Enter A or B, whichever is bigger, or the word equal if neither is.
hints: Both quantities are negative, so squaring does not preserve the direction of a comparison. Work out which square is larger first, then decide what that says.
\(A^2=16+2\sqrt{55}\) and \(B^2=16+2\sqrt{28}\), so \(A^2\gt B^2\). For two negative numbers, the one with the larger square is the smaller number.
blocks.sol: Squaring gives \(A^2=16+2\sqrt{55}\) and \(B^2=16+2\sqrt{28}\), and \(55\gt 28\), so \(A^2\gt B^2\). Both \(A\) and \(B\) are negative, and for negative numbers a larger square means a smaller number, so \(A\lt B\) and the bigger one is \(\boxed{B}\). Squaring is only reversible when both sides are known to be positive, and here running it backwards without that check returns \(A\).

blocks.x: Let \(A=(2m+7)^2+3\) and \(B=3-(m-1)^2\), where \(m\) is any real number. The same one of the two is bigger at every real \(m\). Enter A or B, whichever it is.
hints: Subtract and watch the two \(3\)s cancel. What is left is built only out of squares.
From 8.1, a square of a real number is never negative. These two squares are zero at different values of \(m\), so they are never zero together.
blocks.sol: Subtract. \(A-B=(2m+7)^2+3-3+(m-1)^2=(2m+7)^2+(m-1)^2\), which is zero only if \(2m+7\) and \(m-1\) are both zero, and no single \(m\) is both \(-\frac{7}{2}\) and \(1\). So the difference is positive at every real \(m\) and the bigger one is \(\boxed{A}\). Testing one value of \(m\) would settle only that value, while the sign of the difference settles them all.

blocks.x: Working backwards finds the answer and running forwards proves it. A chain that starts at a guess and ends at a true statement has its steps in the wrong order, so on its own it settles nothing. The same chain has to be written the other way round, one step at a time, with every step valid in that direction. Adding a number to both sides runs both ways, and so does multiplying both sides by a nonzero number of known sign. Squaring runs backwards only when both sides are known to be nonnegative, since \(-3\) and \(3\) have the same square.

Four routes are available, subtracting, rewriting both into a common form, going through a third number, and flipping to reciprocals. Read the shape of the pair first. Nearly identical pieces suit subtracting, matching numerators or bases suit a rewrite, two numbers near a round value suit a middle number, and small fractions suit reciprocals.
Let \(A=\frac{13}{30}\) and \(B=\frac{15}{34}\). Two routes from this lesson settle this pair. Enter A or B, whichever is bigger.
hints: One route subtracts over the common denominator \(1020\). The other flips both and compares the reciprocals.
\(\frac{30}{13}\) and \(\frac{34}{15}\) are each \(2\) plus a fraction, and those two fractions have the same numerator.
blocks.sol: Both are positive, so the bigger number is the one with the smaller reciprocal. \(\frac{1}{A}=\frac{30}{13}=2+\frac{4}{13}\) and \(\frac{1}{B}=\frac{34}{15}=2+\frac{4}{15}\), and those leftovers share a numerator, so \(\frac{4}{13}\gt \frac{4}{15}\) and \(\frac{1}{A}\gt \frac{1}{B}\). The smaller reciprocal is \(\frac{1}{B}\), so the bigger number is \(\boxed{B}\). Subtracting works too, since over the denominator \(1020\) they are \(\frac{442}{1020}\) and \(\frac{450}{1020}\).

blocks.x: Let \(A=7^{18}\) and \(B=18^{12}\). Enter A or B, whichever is bigger, or the word equal if neither is.
hints: Neither base is a power of the other, so a common base is out. Look at the exponents \(18\) and \(12\), which share the factor \(6\).
Write \(7^{18}\) as \((7^3)^6\) and \(18^{12}\) as \((18^2)^6\). Both are sixth powers now, so only the bases \(7^3\) and \(18^2\) have to be compared.
blocks.sol: Both exponents are multiples of \(6\), so write each as a sixth power. Then \(A=(7^3)^6=343^6\) and \(B=(18^2)^6=324^6\), and \(343\gt 324\), so the bigger one is \(\boxed{A}\). \(B\) has the bigger base and \(A\) has the bigger exponent, so neither of those on its own settles the pair.

blocks.x: Every comparison here was between two numbers already fixed. Lesson 8.3, Solving Linear Inequalities, puts a letter on one side and asks which values of that letter make the comparison true. The rules are these same ones, the reversal on multiplying by a negative included.

review.x: Let \(A=\frac{11}{26}\) and \(B=\frac{11}{29}\). Enter A or B, whichever is bigger.
hints: The numerators are already the same, so nothing needs rewriting. Only the denominators differ.
The same \(11\) is cut into \(26\) pieces one way and \(29\) pieces the other, and more pieces means smaller ones.
review.sol: Both fractions have numerator \(11\), and \(26\lt 29\), so \(\frac{11}{26}\) is the bigger number, which makes the answer \(\boxed{A}\). Cutting \(11\) into more equal parts makes each part smaller, so with the numerator fixed the bigger denominator gives the smaller number.

review.x: Let \(A=\frac{5}{9}+\frac{2}{11}\) and \(B=\frac{5}{9}+\frac{3}{14}\). Enter \(A\) or \(B\), whichever is bigger.
hints: Both sums start with \(\frac{5}{9}\). Subtract one from the other and that part is gone.
What is left is \(\frac{2}{11}\) against \(\frac{3}{14}\), and \(2\times 14=28\) against \(3\times 11=33\) settles that.
review.sol: Both carry \(\frac{5}{9}\), so subtracting one from the other removes it. \(A-B=\frac{2}{11}-\frac{3}{14}=\frac{28-33}{154}=-\frac{5}{154}\), which is negative, so the bigger one is \(\boxed{B}\). Neither sum had to be computed.

review.x: Let \(A=3^{15}\) and \(B=9^{7}\cdot 3\). Enter A or B, whichever is bigger, or the word equal if neither is.
hints: \(9\) is a power of \(3\), so \(B\) can be rewritten as a single power of \(3\) and then compared with \(A\) by exponent alone.
Write \(9^7\) as \((3^2)^7\) and multiply the exponents, then add one more for the extra factor of \(3\).
review.sol: Write both as powers of \(3\). \(B=9^7\cdot 3=(3^2)^7\cdot 3=3^{14}\cdot 3=3^{15}\), the same power as \(A\), so the answer is \(\boxed{\text{equal}}\).

review.x: Let \(A=\frac{23}{22}\) and \(B=\frac{21}{24}\). Enter A or B, whichever is bigger.
hints: One of these is above \(1\) and the other is below it.
A fraction of two positive numbers is above \(1\) exactly when its numerator is the bigger of the two. Check \(23\) against \(22\), then \(21\) against \(24\).
review.sol: Compare each with \(1\). Since \(23\gt 22\), \(A\gt 1\), and since \(21\lt 24\), \(B\lt 1\), so \(A\gt 1\gt B\) and the bigger one is \(\boxed{A}\).

review.x: Let \(A=46\times 54\) and \(B=50^2\). Enter A or B, whichever is bigger, or the word equal if neither is.
hints: Neither product has to be multiplied out in full. Try splitting each one into two pieces that overlap.
\(46\times 54=46\times 50+46\times 4\) and \(50^2=46\times 50+4\times 50\), and the first piece is the same in both.
review.sol: Splitting each product the same way gives \(46\times 54=46\times 50+184\) and \(50^2=46\times 50+200\), so the bigger one is \(\boxed{B}\). The shared \(46\times 50\) never has to be worked out, only \(184\) against \(200\).

review.x: Let \(A=-\frac{1}{6}\) and \(B=-\frac{1}{13}\). Enter A or B, whichever is bigger, or the word unknown if it cannot be decided.
hints: Both are negative. Compare \(\frac{1}{6}\) with \(\frac{1}{13}\) first.
\(\frac{1}{6}\gt \frac{1}{13}\), and negating both sides of a comparison reverses it.
review.sol: Both are negative, and \(\frac{1}{6}\gt \frac{1}{13}\), so negating reverses that to \(-\frac{1}{6}\lt -\frac{1}{13}\) and the bigger one is \(\boxed{B}\). Multiplying by \(-1\) is the reversal from 8.1.

review.x: Let \(v\) be any real number, with \(A=(v-8)^2+3\) and \(B=2\). Enter A or B, whichever is bigger.
hints: The comparison has to hold for every real \(v\), so start by finding the smallest value \((v-8)^2\) can take.
Put \((v-8)^2\) at that smallest value and read off \(A\) there. If \(A\) is above \(B\) even at its smallest, the comparison is settled for every \(v\).
review.sol: A square is never negative, so \((v-8)^2+3\) is at least \(3\), and \(3\) is more than \(2\), which makes the bigger quantity \(\boxed{A}\). Checking \(A\) at its smallest is enough here, since a quantity whose smallest value is above \(B\) is above \(B\) at every \(v\).

review.x: Let \(A=\frac{3}{50}\) and \(B=\frac{4}{67}\). Enter the letter \(A\) or \(B\), whichever is bigger.
hints: Both are positive, so the bigger one has the smaller reciprocal. Compare \(\frac{1}{A}\) and \(\frac{1}{B}\) instead.
\(\frac{1}{A}=\frac{50}{3}=16+\frac{2}{3}\) and \(\frac{1}{B}=\frac{67}{4}=16+\frac{3}{4}\), so only the leftover fractions matter.
review.sol: Both are positive, so the bigger number has the smaller reciprocal. \(\frac{1}{A}=\frac{50}{3}=16+\frac{2}{3}\) and \(\frac{1}{B}=\frac{67}{4}=16+\frac{3}{4}\), and \(\frac{2}{3}\lt \frac{3}{4}\), so \(\frac{1}{A}\lt \frac{1}{B}\) and the bigger one is \(\boxed{A}\). Cross-multiplying settles it too, since \(3\cdot 67=201\) is more than \(4\cdot 50=200\).

review.x: Let \(A=\frac{337}{676}\) and \(B=\frac{449}{897}\). Enter A or B, whichever is bigger.
hints: Six-digit cross-multiplication is the slow route. Compare each with \(\frac{1}{2}\) instead.
A positive fraction beats \(\frac{1}{2}\) exactly when twice its numerator beats its denominator. Double \(337\), then double \(449\).
review.sol: Compare each with \(\frac{1}{2}\). Doubling the numerators gives \(674\lt 676\) and \(898\gt 897\), so \(A\lt \frac{1}{2}\lt B\) and the bigger one is \(\boxed{B}\).

review.x: Let \(A=\sqrt{10}+\sqrt{14}\) and \(B=\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{22}\). Enter A or B, whichever is bigger, or the word equal if neither is.
hints: Assume one is bigger and square both sides. Both quantities are positive, so that step can be run backwards afterwards.
Squaring gives \(24+2\sqrt{140}\) against \(24+2\sqrt{44}\), so only the two products under the radicals have to be compared.
review.sol: Both are positive, so squaring preserves the comparison. \(A^2=10+14+2\sqrt{140}=24+2\sqrt{140}\) and \(B^2=2+22+2\sqrt{44}=24+2\sqrt{44}\), and \(140\gt 44\), so \(A^2\gt B^2\) and the bigger one is \(\boxed{A}\). The two sums have the same total under the radicals, so the pair with the closer parts is the larger sum.

review.x: Enter how many of these five statements are true. $$\text{(1) } \frac{5}{12}\gt \frac{5}{13}\qquad\text{(2) } 2^{10}\gt 10^{3}\qquad\text{(3) } -\frac{3}{4}\gt -\frac{2}{3}$$ $$\text{(4) } \frac{1}{-11}\gt \frac{1}{-6}\qquad\text{(5) } \frac{7}{15}\lt \frac{1}{2}$$
hints: Take them one at a time and use the shortest route for each. Two of the five put the same numerator over different denominators, one is a pair of powers, and one gives way to a common denominator. The negatives are where the direction is easiest to lose.
\(2^{10}=1024\) and \(10^3=1000\). For the negatives, compare \(\frac{3}{4}\) with \(\frac{2}{3}\) first, then \(\frac{1}{11}\) with \(\frac{1}{6}\).
review.sol: Only statement 3 fails, since \(\frac{3}{4}\gt \frac{2}{3}\) and multiplying both sides by \(-1\) reverses that to \(-\frac{3}{4}\lt -\frac{2}{3}\). The other four hold, by the same numerator over the smaller denominator in 1, by \(1024\gt 1000\) in 2, by \(-\frac{1}{11}\gt -\frac{1}{6}\) in 4, and by \(\frac{14}{30}\lt \frac{15}{30}\) in 5, so the count is \(\boxed{4}\).

review.x: Let \(u=-\frac{5}{6}\) and \(v=\frac{4}{3}\), and let \(A=\frac{1}{u}\) and \(B=\frac{1}{v}\). Enter A or B, whichever is bigger, or the word unknown if it cannot be decided.
hints: Before reaching for the reciprocal rule, check the condition it needs, that \(u\) and \(v\) have the same sign.
Flipping a fraction takes one step, so compute \(A\) and \(B\) outright and compare the two values.
review.sol: Flip each one. \(A=\frac{1}{u}=-\frac{6}{5}\) and \(B=\frac{1}{v}=\frac{3}{4}\), and a negative value is less than a positive one, so the bigger one is \(\boxed{B}\). The reciprocal rule needs \(u\) and \(v\) on the same side of zero, and they are not, so comparing the two values directly is the reliable route.

review.x: Let \(n\) be a nonzero real number, with nothing else known about it, and let \(A=\frac{9}{n}\) and \(B=\frac{5}{n}\). Enter A or B, whichever is bigger, or the word unknown if it cannot be decided.
hints: Compare by subtracting. \(A-B=\frac{4}{n}\), so the answer depends only on the sign of that fraction.
Try \(n=2\), then try \(n=-2\).
review.sol: At \(n=2\) the values are \(\frac{9}{2}\) and \(\frac{5}{2}\), so \(A\) is bigger, while at \(n=-2\) they are \(-\frac{9}{2}\) and \(-\frac{5}{2}\), so \(B\) is bigger, leaving the answer \(\boxed{\text{unknown}}\). Subtracting settles it the same way, since the sign of \(A-B=\frac{4}{n}\) is the sign of \(n\), and no sign is given.

review.x: Let \(A=\frac{27}{40}\) and \(B=\frac{19}{28}\). Multiplying both by \(280\) clears both denominators. Enter A or B, whichever is bigger.
hints: \(280\) is positive, so multiplying both by \(280\) leaves the order unchanged, which means the two products compare the same way as \(A\) and \(B\).
\(\frac{280}{40}=7\) and \(\frac{280}{28}=10\), so the two products are \(7\times 27\) and \(10\times 19\).
review.sol: Multiplying by \(280\) gives \(7\times 27=189\) for \(A\) and \(10\times 19=190\) for \(B\), so the bigger one is \(\boxed{B}\). Since \(280\) is positive, the order is the same before and after the scaling, so \(189<190\) settles the original pair.

review.x: Enter the smallest integer \(n\) for which \(2^{n}\gt 5^{7}\).
hints: Work out \(5^7\) first, then find where the powers of \(2\) cross it.
review.sol: \(5^7=78125\), and \(2^{16}=65536\) is less than that while \(2^{17}=131072\) is greater, so the smallest such integer is \(\boxed{17}\). A middle number like \(10^5\) settles the upper end at once, since \(2^{17}\gt 10^5\gt 5^7\), but it cannot settle the lower end, because \(2^{16}\) and \(5^7\) are both below it.

review.x: Let \(A=\frac{8}{17}\) and \(B=\frac{9}{19}\). Enter A or B, whichever is bigger.
hints: The two are close, so compare each one to \(\frac{1}{2}\) first. Doubling the numerator and checking it against the denominator tells you which side of \(\frac{1}{2}\) a fraction sits on.
That check leaves both on the same side, so it settles nothing. Subtract one from the other over the common denominator \(17\times 19=323\) and read the sign of the result.
review.sol: Over the common denominator \(17\times 19=323\), \(\frac{9}{19}-\frac{8}{17}=\frac{9\times 17-8\times 19}{323}=\frac{153-152}{323}=\frac{1}{323}\), which is positive, so the bigger one is \(\boxed{B}\). Comparing each to \(\frac{1}{2}\) is no help, since doubling the numerators gives \(16\lt 17\) and \(18\lt 19\), so both fractions are below \(\frac{1}{2}\).

review.x: Let \(A=\frac{1}{2^{45}}\) and \(B=\frac{1}{5^{18}}\). Enter A or B, whichever is bigger.
hints: Both fractions have numerator \(1\), so the one with the smaller denominator is the bigger number, and the question becomes which of \(2^{45}\) and \(5^{18}\) is smaller.
Neither power can be worked out by hand, so give the two a common exponent. Both \(45\) and \(18\) are multiples of \(9\), so power of a power from 3.1 rewrites each one as a ninth power.
review.sol: Both have numerator \(1\), so the smaller denominator gives the bigger fraction. Power of a power rewrites \(2^{45}=(2^{5})^{9}=32^{9}\) and \(5^{18}=(5^{2})^{9}=25^{9}\), so \(5^{18}\lt 2^{45}\) and the bigger fraction is \(\boxed{B}\). A common exponent works whenever the two exponents share a factor, since it leaves only the bases to compare.

blocks.x: An inequality with a letter in it is true at some values of that letter and false at others. Solving it means finding every value that makes it true. The moves are the ones chapter 4 used to solve equations, run under 8.1's rules, and one of those rules is the reason an inequality is not just an equation with a different symbol.
Every solution of \(y-23\ge 46\) sits at or above a single number, and that number is itself a solution. Enter that number.
hints: The boundary is the \(y\) that makes \(y-23\) exactly \(46\), and it counts as a solution because \(\ge\) is true when the two sides are equal.
Undo the subtraction. Adding \(23\) to both sides is one of 8.1's moves that leaves the direction alone, so it clears the \(-23\) off the left.
blocks.sol: Adding \(23\) to both sides gives \(y\ge \boxed{69}\). Adding the same amount to both sides leaves the direction alone. At \(y=69\) the left side is exactly \(46\), which counts, and at \(y=68\) it is \(45\), which does not.

blocks.x: The solutions of \(6w+19\lt 91\) are exactly the numbers less than one cutoff value, and the cutoff itself is not a solution. Enter the cutoff value.
hints: Two moves, in the same order chapter 4 used on equations. Clear the \(19\) first, then the coefficient \(6\).
Subtracting \(19\) from both sides leaves \(6w\lt 72\). Six is positive, so the direction of the inequality stays the same when you divide both sides by it.
blocks.sol: Subtract \(19\) from both sides for \(6w\lt 72\), then divide by the positive \(6\) for \(w\lt \boxed{12}\). At \(w=12\) the left side is exactly \(91\), and \(91\lt 91\) is false, so \(12\) is the cutoff and not a solution.

blocks.x: Solving an inequality means describing every value that makes it true. The equation \(6w+19=91\) holds at \(w=12\) and at no other value, so the whole answer is one number. The inequality \(6w+19\lt 91\) holds at \(11\), at \(0\), at \(-800\), and at every number below \(12\), so the solutions cannot be listed. The answer is a description instead, the single simple inequality \(w\lt 12\), which is a boundary and a direction and nothing else. Producing that form is the goal of every problem here, the way \(w=12\) was the goal in chapter 4.
Enter the largest integer \(t\) that satisfies \(4t-9\lt 50\).
hints: Describe all the solutions first, then pick the largest integer inside that description.
Adding \(9\) gives \(4t\lt 59\), and dividing by \(4\) leaves a boundary that is not a whole number. Test the whole number just below it.
blocks.sol: Add \(9\) to both sides for \(4t\lt 59\), then divide by the positive \(4\) for \(t\lt \frac{59}{4}\). Since \(\frac{59}{4}=14.75\), the largest integer allowed is \(\boxed{14}\). Checking, \(4(14)-9=47\) is below \(50\) while \(4(15)-9=51\) is not. The boundary is not a whole number, so no integer sits exactly on it and \(\le\) in place of \(\lt\) would give the same answer.

blocks.x: A student solves \(11-4x\le 49\). After subtracting \(11\) from both sides, the student divides by \(-4\) and leaves the symbol pointing the same way, which makes the resulting statement about \(x\) wrong. Enter the largest integer that fits the student's wrong statement.
hints: Follow the student's work rather than your own. Subtracting \(11\) gives \(-4x\le 38\), and the student then divides by \(-4\) while keeping \(\le\).
The student's statement is \(x\le -\frac{19}{2}\), and \(-\frac{19}{2}=-9.5\). No integer equals \(-9.5\), so take the largest integer below it, and on the negative side larger means closer to zero.
blocks.sol: Subtracting \(11\) gives \(-4x\le 38\), and dividing by \(-4\) without reversing gives \(x\le -\frac{19}{2}\), so the student's largest integer is \(\boxed{-10}\). Dividing by a negative reverses the symbol, so the true statement is \(x\ge -\frac{19}{2}\) and the smallest integer that works is \(-9\). Testing \(x=-10\) in the original gives \(11+40=51\), above \(49\).

blocks.x: Isolate the variable exactly as in chapter 4. Undo the last operation first, clearing the constant by adding or subtracting and then clearing the coefficient by dividing, which is 4.2's order. Adding or subtracting the same amount on both sides never changes the direction, and neither does multiplying or dividing by a positive number. Multiplying or dividing both sides by a negative number reverses the direction, which is 8.1's rule and the only difference from solving an equation. Dividing \(-4x\le 38\) by \(-4\) gives \(x\ge -\frac{19}{2}\), not \(x\le -\frac{19}{2}\).
