blocks.cap: Here \(a\) is a positive number, so \(-a\) is negative. The two ladders show the same two steps. Subtracting \(b\) leaves the direction alone in each. The last step is where the direction can change, and it changes only when the divisor is negative. Dividing by \(a\) keeps \(\gt\), and dividing by \(-a\) reverses it to \(\lt\).

blocks.x: A negative coefficient is not forced on you. When the variable is on both sides, a variable term can be removed from either side, and one of those two removals leaves a positive coefficient behind. Removing a variable term is a subtraction, so it never reverses the direction. That choice comes up in each of the next two problems.
Enter the smallest integer \(k\) that satisfies \(9k-14\gt 5k+26\).
hints: Once \(k\) has a value, \(5k\) is a number, so subtracting \(5k\) from both sides is 4.3's move and the direction holds.
That leaves \(4k-14\gt 26\). Add \(14\), divide by \(4\), then take the smallest integer strictly above the boundary.
blocks.sol: Subtract \(5k\) from both sides for \(4k-14\gt 26\), add \(14\) for \(4k\gt 40\), then divide by \(4\) for \(k\gt 10\), so the smallest integer is \(\boxed{11}\). At \(k=10\) both sides equal \(76\), and \(\gt\) does not allow equality.

blocks.x: In \(3m+47\le 8m+12\) the variable terms can be gathered on either side. Use the choice that leaves a positive coefficient, so no reversal is needed. Enter the smallest value \(m\) can take.
hints: Subtracting \(3m\) from both sides puts the variable on the right with a positive coefficient. Subtracting \(8m\) instead leaves \(-5m\) on the left, so a division by a negative comes later.
Take the first route. Subtracting \(3m\) and then \(12\) from both sides gives \(35\le 5m\).
blocks.sol: Subtract \(3m\) from both sides for \(47\le 5m+12\), subtract \(12\) for \(35\le 5m\), and divide by the positive \(5\) for \(7\le m\), so the smallest value is \(\boxed{7}\). Gathering on the left instead gives \(-5m\le -35\), and dividing by \(-5\) reverses the symbol to \(m\ge 7\). Both routes describe the same solutions, but the second has one more step where the direction can be lost.

blocks.x: Gather the variable terms onto one side, and choose that side. Once the letter has a value, a term such as \(5m\) is a number, so subtracting it from both sides is 4.3's move and the direction holds. Both choices are legal and both give the same description. Subtract the smaller variable term. In \(3m+47\le 8m+12\) that means subtracting \(3m\), which leaves \(5m\) on the right and a final division by \(5\). Subtracting \(8m\) instead leaves \(-5m\) on the left and a final division by \(-5\), which is one more place to lose the direction.

Isolating comes last. Distribute to clear parentheses the 2.1 way, and combine like terms on each side the 2.4 way. Neither move changes the other side, so no question of direction comes up while a side is being cleaned. Clean both sides first, then gather the variable terms and isolate.
Enter the largest integer \(x\) that satisfies \(7(2x-5)-3x\lt 4(x+8)+6\).
hints: Simplify each side before gathering anything. Distribute both products, then combine like terms on each side separately.
The two sides become \(11x-35\) and \(4x+38\). Subtract \(4x\) rather than \(11x\), since taking away the smaller coefficient leaves a positive coefficient on \(x\).
blocks.sol: Distributing and combining gives \(11x-35\lt 4x+38\). Subtracting \(4x\) gives \(7x-35\lt 38\), adding \(35\) gives \(7x\lt 73\), and dividing by \(7\) gives \(x\lt \frac{73}{7}\). Since \(\frac{73}{7}\) sits between \(10\) and \(11\), the largest integer is \(\boxed{10}\). Distributing multiplies both terms inside the parentheses by \(7\), so \(7(2x-5)\) is \(14x-35\) and not \(14x-5\).

blocks.x: Joseph Fourier published a method in 1826 for taking a whole system of linear inequalities and removing one unknown at a time from it, the same elimination idea 5.3 used on systems of equations.
The inequality \(\frac{3x}{4}-\frac{x}{6}\ge 21\) is true for every \(x\) from one value upward, and that value itself makes it true. Clear the fractions first, then enter that value.
hints: The two denominators are \(4\) and \(6\). Multiplying both sides by a number that both of them divide leaves no fraction anywhere.
Multiplying by \(12\) gives \(9x-2x\ge 252\), and \(12\) is positive, so the direction is unchanged.
blocks.sol: Multiply both sides by \(12\), a positive number, so the direction is unchanged, giving \(9x-2x\ge 252\), then \(7x\ge 252\) and \(x\ge \boxed{36}\). Checking the endpoint, \(\frac{3(36)}{4}-\frac{36}{6}=27-6=21\), and \(21\ge 21\) is true, so \(36\) itself is a solution.

blocks.x: Simplify each side before gathering anything. Distributing and combining like terms rewrite one side as an equal expression, so the other side and the direction are unchanged. Clear fractions by multiplying both sides by a positive common denominator. A common denominator is positive by choice, so that step never reverses the direction. Multiplying \(\frac{3x}{4}-\frac{x}{6}\ge 21\) by \(12\) gives \(9x-2x\ge 252\), with \(\ge\) pointing the same way. Multiplying by a negative number instead would clear the fractions and reverse every symbol, so there is no reason to do it.

Gathering the variable terms can remove every one of them, since the two sides can have the same variable part. What is left is a comparison between two numbers with no letter in it. A comparison like that reads the same at every value, true as it stands or false as it stands, so the original holds everywhere or nowhere.

The statement \(-13\le 4x+7\lt 39\) is a chain, and it says both \(-13\le 4x+7\) and \(4x+7\lt 39\) at once. Solve it by doing the same thing to all three parts at each step. Enter the smallest value of \(x\) that makes the whole chain true.
hints: The middle part is \(4x+7\), so the first move is subtracting \(7\), and that subtraction has to be done to \(-13\) and to \(39\) as well.
Subtracting \(7\) from all three parts gives \(-20\le 4x\lt 32\). Dividing all three by \(4\) is dividing by a positive number, so both directions hold.
blocks.sol: Subtract \(7\) from all three parts for \(-20\le 4x\lt 32\), then divide all three by the positive \(4\) for \(-5\le x\lt 8\), so the smallest value is \(\boxed{-5}\). Checking, \(4(-5)+7=-13\), and \(-13\le -13\lt 39\) is true. Any \(x\) below \(-5\) makes \(4x+7\) less than \(-13\), so the left comparison fails.

blocks.x: Enter how many of the values \(x=-31\), \(x=-\frac{5}{6}\), \(x=0\), \(x=4.5\), \(x=57\) and \(x=210\) satisfy \(5(x+9)-2x\gt 3x+38\).
hints: Testing each value one at a time is the long route. Simplify the left side and gather the variable terms first, then see what is left.
The left side collects to \(3x+45\), so both sides carry \(3x\). Subtracting \(3x\) removes the letter entirely.
blocks.sol: Distributing gives \(5x+45-2x=3x+45\) on the left, so the inequality is \(3x+45\gt 3x+38\). Subtracting \(3x\) from both sides leaves \(45\gt 38\), which is true and contains no \(x\), so every real number is a solution and the count is \(\boxed{6}\). A true numerical statement at the end means the inequality holds everywhere, whatever the listed values happened to be.

blocks.x: When every variable term cancels, the numerical statement left behind is the whole answer. If it is true, such as \(45\gt 38\), the original holds at every real number and every value is a solution. If it is false, such as \(-6\gt 9\), the original holds nowhere and there are no solutions. These are 4.3's two endings for equations, the identity and the no-solutions case, reached the same way and read the same way. Watch for the lookalike. If a variable term remains, nothing special has happened and the inequality is an ordinary one.

Check a finished description with two substitutions. Put the boundary value into the original and see whether it holds, which settles whether the boundary itself counts. Then test one value from the described side. A missed reversal shows up on that second test, since with the direction backwards every value in the description fails the original.
Enter how many integers \(x\) with \(-15\le x\le 15\) satisfy \(9-2x\gt 3x-31\). The inequality on its own has infinitely many integer solutions, so only the ones inside the stated range are counted.
hints: Both sides have an \(x\) term, so gather them on one side before anything else. Collect them where the coefficient comes out positive and no step will divide by a negative.

Adding \(2x\) and then \(31\) to both sides gives \(40\gt 5x\). That sets only the top of the allowed range, since the bottom is the stated \(-15\). The symbol is strict, so check whether the cutoff value itself counts.
blocks.sol: Adding \(2x\) and \(31\) to both sides gives \(40\gt 5x\), so \(x\lt 8\). Inside \(-15\le x\le 15\) the allowed integers run from \(-15\) to \(7\), and \(7-(-15)+1=\boxed{23}\). Checking, \(x=7\) gives \(-5\gt -10\), true, and \(x=8\) gives \(-7\gt -7\), false. Adding \(2x\) rather than subtracting \(3x\) keeps the coefficient positive and removes the reversal step.

blocks.x: Enter how many integers \(x\) satisfy \(-7\lt \frac{13-3x}{2}\le 5\). Both ends of the solved form are integers, so test each one in the original inequality before counting.
hints: Clear the fraction first by multiplying all three parts by \(2\). That multiplier is positive, so neither direction reverses.
Subtracting \(13\) from all three parts leaves \(-27\lt -3x\le -3\). Dividing all three by \(-3\) reverses both directions, so the \(\le\) end becomes the lower end.
blocks.sol: Multiplying all three parts by \(2\) gives \(-14\lt 13-3x\le 10\), subtracting \(13\) gives \(-27\lt -3x\le -3\), and dividing all three by \(-3\) reverses both directions to \(9\gt x\ge 1\), which reads \(1\le x\lt 9\). The integers are \(1\) through \(8\), so the count is \(\boxed{8}\). Test both ends in the original. At \(x=1\) the middle part is \(5\), and \(5\le 5\) is true, so \(1\) is in. At \(x=9\) the middle part is \(-7\), and \(-7\lt -7\) is false, so \(9\) is out.

blocks.x: Every answer here was described in words and symbols, a boundary together with the direction that goes with it. Lesson 8.4, Graphing Inequalities, is where those descriptions are drawn instead. On a number line the boundary is one marked point and the solutions are everything on one side of it, and with two letters the picture is a region of the plane.

review.x: A number \(x\) satisfies \(x+38\le 55\). Enter the largest value \(x\) can be.
hints: Subtracting \(38\) from both sides leaves the direction alone.
\(\le\) means less than or equal to, so the boundary value itself satisfies the inequality.
review.sol: Subtracting \(38\) from both sides leaves the direction unchanged, giving \(x\le \boxed{17}\). Since \(\le\) means less than or equal to, \(x=17\) is allowed, and checking, \(17+38=55\).

review.x: Enter the smallest integer \(p\) that satisfies \(\frac{p}{5}+7\gt 16\).
hints: Subtract \(7\) from both sides first. Subtracting the same amount from both sides leaves the direction unchanged.
That leaves \(\frac{p}{5}\gt 9\). Multiply both sides by the positive \(5\), then check whether the boundary value itself satisfies the strict inequality.
review.sol: Subtracting \(7\) gives \(\frac{p}{5}\gt 9\), and multiplying both sides by the positive \(5\) gives \(p\gt 45\), so the smallest integer is \(\boxed{46}\). At \(p=45\) the left side equals \(16\) exactly, which is not greater than \(16\).

review.x: Enter the smallest integer \(x\) that satisfies \(-3x\lt 24\).
hints: The coefficient is negative, so the last step is a division by a negative number.
Dividing by \(-3\) reverses the symbol to \(x\gt -8\), and \(-8\) itself is excluded.
review.sol: Dividing both sides by \(-3\) reverses the direction to \(x\gt -8\), so the smallest integer is \(\boxed{-7}\). Checking, \(-3(-7)=21\lt 24\) while \(-3(-8)=24\) is not below \(24\).

review.x: Solve \(5k-24\ge 71\). The solutions are exactly the values of \(k\) at or above a single number, and that number is itself a solution. Enter that number.
hints: Add \(24\) to both sides, then divide both sides by \(5\). Both moves leave the direction alone, since \(5\) is positive.
The first move gives \(5k\ge 95\). Since the sign is \(\ge\) and not \(\gt\), the boundary value is itself a solution.
review.sol: Adding \(24\) to both sides gives \(5k\ge 95\), and dividing both sides by \(5\) leaves the direction alone, so \(k\ge \boxed{19}\). At \(k=19\) the left side is exactly \(71\), and \(\ge\) includes that boundary.

review.x: Enter the largest integer \(y\) that satisfies \(8y+11\lt 122\).
hints: Solve for \(y\) first, then take the largest integer that still fits below the bound you get.
Subtracting \(11\) gives \(8y\lt 111\), and \(\frac{111}{8}\) is not a whole number.
review.sol: Subtracting \(11\) gives \(8y\lt 111\), and dividing by \(8\) gives \(y\lt \frac{111}{8}=13.875\), so the largest integer is \(\boxed{13}\). Checking, \(8(13)+11=115\lt 122\) while \(8(14)+11=123\) is not below \(122\).

review.x: A number \(x\) satisfies \(20-4x\ge 52\). Enter the largest value \(x\) can be.
hints: Subtract \(20\) from both sides first, and leave the negative coefficient for the last step.
That gives \(-4x\ge 32\). Dividing both sides by \(-4\) reverses the direction, and the boundary value itself still counts, since the comparison is \(\ge\).
review.sol: Subtracting \(20\) gives \(-4x\ge 32\), and dividing by \(-4\) reverses the direction to \(x\le \boxed{-8}\). At \(x=-8\) the left side is \(20-4(-8)=52\), which is allowed since the comparison is \(\ge\), while \(x=-7\) gives \(48\). Skipping the reversal would give \(x\ge -8\), which is false at \(x=0\), where the left side is \(20\).

review.x: Enter the smallest integer \(v\) that satisfies \(12v-5\gt 5v+100\).
hints: Subtract \(5v\) from both sides, which leaves the variable on the left with a positive coefficient.
That gives \(7v-5\gt 100\), so \(7v\gt 105\).
review.sol: Subtracting \(5v\) gives \(7v-5\gt 100\), adding \(5\) gives \(7v\gt 105\), and dividing by \(7\) gives \(v\gt 15\), so the smallest integer is \(\boxed{16}\). At \(v=15\) both sides equal \(175\), and the bound is strict, so \(15\) is ruled out.

review.x: Enter how many integers \(n\) with \(-10\le n\le 30\) satisfy \(4n-9\lt 3n+13\).
hints: Solve first, then count. Subtracting \(3n\) leaves a coefficient of \(1\).
The condition is \(n\lt 22\), so the allowed integers stop at \(21\) and start at the lower end of the stated range.
review.sol: Subtracting \(3n\) gives \(n-9\lt 13\), so \(n\lt 22\). Inside \(-10\le n\le 30\) the integers allowed run from \(-10\) to \(21\), and \(21-(-10)+1=\boxed{32}\). Subtracting the two endpoints without adding \(1\) gives \(31\) and misses one of the two ends.

review.x: Enter the largest value of \(x\) that satisfies \(6x+5\le 4x+12\), as a fraction in lowest terms.
hints: Subtract \(4x\) from both sides rather than \(6x\), since taking away the smaller variable term keeps the coefficient of \(x\) positive.
That gives \(2x+5\le 12\), so \(2x\le 7\). The boundary is not a whole number.
review.sol: Subtracting \(4x\) gives \(2x+5\le 12\), subtracting \(5\) gives \(2x\le 7\), and dividing by the positive number \(2\) keeps the direction, giving \(x\le \boxed{\frac{7}{2}}\). Both sides equal \(26\) at \(x=\frac{7}{2}\), and since the comparison is \(\le \) rather than \(\lt \), that boundary value is itself a solution.

review.x: The inequality \(3(2x+7)-5x\ge 2(x-4)+9\) holds for every \(x\) at or below one value, and that value satisfies it too. Enter that value.
hints: Distribute on both sides and combine like terms before moving any term across the inequality sign.

The two sides simplify to \(x+21\) and \(2x+1\). Subtract \(x\) from both sides to clear the smaller variable term, and note that subtracting the same amount from both sides never changes the direction.
review.sol: Distributing and combining gives \(x+21\ge 2x+1\). Subtracting \(x\) from both sides gives \(21\ge x+1\), and subtracting \(1\) gives \(20\ge x\), so \(x\le \boxed{20}\). At \(x=20\) both sides equal \(41\), and a \(\ge\) statement is true when the two sides are equal, so \(20\) itself is a solution.

review.x: Solve \(\frac{x}{3}+\frac{x}{4}\gt 14\). Enter the largest number that is not a solution.
hints: Multiply both sides by \(12\), which clears both denominators and is a positive multiplier.
That gives \(4x+3x\gt 168\), so \(7x\gt 168\).
review.sol: Multiplying both sides by the positive number \(12\) keeps the direction, giving \(4x+3x\gt 168\), so \(7x\gt 168\) and \(x\gt \boxed{24}\). Every number above \(24\) is a solution and \(24\) is not, since at \(x=24\) the left side is \(8+6=14\), which is not greater than \(14\).

review.x: Enter the smallest integer \(x\) that satisfies \(-11\lt 5x+4\le 34\).
hints: This is two conditions at once, \(-11\lt 5x+4\) and \(5x+4\le 34\), and only the left one limits how small \(x\) can be. Take the \(+4\) off all three parts in one step.
Subtracting \(4\) from all three gives \(-15\lt 5x\le 30\). The left end is strict, so the boundary there is excluded.
review.sol: Subtracting \(4\) from all three parts gives \(-15\lt 5x\le 30\), and dividing all three by the positive \(5\) gives \(-3\lt x\le 6\), so the smallest integer is \(\boxed{-2}\). The left end is strict, so \(-3\) is excluded even though \(5(-3)+4=-11\) sits right at it.

review.x: Enter the largest integer \(x\) that satisfies \(1\le 8-3x\lt 20\).
hints: Subtract \(8\) from all three parts, then handle the negative coefficient.
That gives \(-7\le -3x\lt 12\). Dividing all three parts by \(-3\) reverses both symbols.
review.sol: Subtracting \(8\) from all three parts gives \(-7\le -3x\lt 12\), and dividing all three by \(-3\) reverses both symbols to \(\frac{7}{3}\ge x\gt -4\), which reads \(-4\lt x\le \frac{7}{3}\). The largest integer is \(\boxed{2}\). Checking, \(8-3(2)=2\) satisfies the chain while \(8-3(3)=-1\) falls below \(1\).

review.x: Test the five values \(x=-30\), \(x=-\frac{1}{2}\), \(x=6.5\), \(x=41\) and \(x=88\) in \(7(x-2)-3x\ge 4x+5\). Enter how many of them satisfy the inequality.
hints: Simplify the left side and gather the variable terms before testing anything.
The left side collects to \(4x-14\), so both sides carry \(4x\). Subtracting \(4x\) from both sides removes the letter.
review.sol: Distributing gives \(7x-14-3x=4x-14\), so the inequality reads \(4x-14\ge 4x+5\). Subtracting \(4x\) from both sides leaves \(-14\ge 5\), which is false, so no value of \(x\) works and the count is \(\boxed{0}\). Once the variable cancels and a false number statement is left, the inequality has no solutions no matter which values are tested.

review.x: A student solves \(3(8-2x)\gt x-41\). After distributing and gathering the variable terms on the left, the student divides by the negative coefficient and keeps the symbol pointing the same way. Enter the largest integer that actually satisfies the original inequality.
hints: Distributing on the left gives \(24-6x\). Put \(x=10\) into both sides of the original and compare the two results.
Subtracting \(x\) and then \(24\) from both sides gives \(-7x\gt -65\), and dividing by \(-7\) reverses the direction, so the solutions sit below the boundary rather than above it.
review.sol: Distributing gives \(24-6x\gt x-41\), subtracting \(x\) and \(24\) from both sides gives \(-7x\gt -65\), and dividing by \(-7\) reverses the direction to \(x\lt \frac{65}{7}\), so the largest integer is \(\boxed{9}\). Checking, \(x=9\) gives \(-30\gt -32\) while \(x=10\) gives \(-36\gt -31\), which is false. Without the reversal the description comes out as \(x\gt \frac{65}{7}\), the same boundary pointing the wrong way.

review.x: Enter the largest integer \(x\) that satisfies \(\frac{2x-1}{3}-\frac{x+2}{5}\lt \frac{x}{15}+1\).
hints: Multiply every term by \(15\), which clears all three denominators at once and is a positive multiplier.
That gives \(5(2x-1)-3(x+2)\lt x+15\). The \(-3\) multiplies the \(+2\) as well.
review.sol: Multiplying by the positive \(15\) gives \(5(2x-1)-3(x+2)\lt x+15\), which is \(7x-11\lt x+15\). Subtracting \(x\) and adding \(11\) gives \(6x\lt 26\), so \(x\lt \frac{13}{3}\) and the largest integer is \(\boxed{4}\). Distributing \(-3\) over \(x+2\) gives \(-3x-6\). Writing \(+6\) there instead changes the boundary and the answer with it.

review.x: Enter how many integers \(x\) satisfy \(-6\le \frac{5-2x}{4}\lt 3\).
hints: Multiply all three parts by \(4\) first. That multiplier is positive, so both directions stay as they are.
That gives \(-24\le 5-2x\lt 12\), and subtracting \(5\) gives \(-29\le -2x\lt 7\). Dividing all three parts by \(-2\) reverses both directions.
review.sol: Multiplying all three parts by \(4\) gives \(-24\le 5-2x\lt 12\), subtracting \(5\) gives \(-29\le -2x\lt 7\), and dividing all three parts by \(-2\) reverses both directions to \(\frac{29}{2}\ge x\gt -\frac{7}{2}\), which reads \(-\frac{7}{2}\lt x\le \frac{29}{2}\). The integers run from \(-3\) to \(14\), so the count is \(14-(-3)+1=\boxed{18}\). Both boundaries are fractions here, so no integer sits exactly on either end.

blocks.x: A solved inequality is a boundary together with a direction, and drawing it means being exact about both, which side of the boundary the solutions lie on and whether the boundary itself is one of them. On a number line those are a direction and a single circle, and in the plane they are a side of a line together with how that line is drawn.
The solutions of \(4x+7\ge 83\) fill a ray on the number line, running right from a single point. Enter the number where the ray starts.
hints: The point at the end of the ray is the value where the two sides come out exactly equal, so start by solving.
Subtracting \(7\) from both sides leaves \(4x\ge 76\), and \(4\) is positive, so dividing by it leaves the direction alone.
blocks.sol: Subtract \(7\) from both sides for \(4x\ge 76\), then divide by the positive \(4\) for \(x\ge \boxed{19}\). At \(x=19\) the left side is exactly \(83\), and \(83\ge 83\) is true, so the ray starts at \(19\) and includes that point.

blocks.x: On a number line the endpoint of a solution ray is drawn as an open circle when that endpoint is not a solution and as a filled circle when it is. Solve \(6x+13\gt 55\), put the boundary number you get back into the inequality, and enter the word, open or filled, for the circle at that endpoint.
hints: The circle at the endpoint answers one yes or no question, whether the boundary number itself satisfies \(6x+13\gt 55\).
Isolating \(x\) gives \(x\gt 7\), so the endpoint is \(7\). Put \(7\) into the left side and compare what you get against \(55\) under a strict \(\gt\).
blocks.sol: Subtracting \(13\) gives \(6x\gt 42\), and dividing by \(6\) gives \(x\gt 7\). Putting \(7\) back in gives \(55\gt 55\), which is false, so \(7\) is not a solution and its circle is \(\boxed{\text{open}}\). Everything to the right of \(7\) is shaded and \(7\) itself is not. With \(\ge\) in place of \(\gt\), that one point would be a solution and the circle would be filled.

blocks.x: On a number line the graph of an inequality is a ray, with a circle at its end. The graph is every point whose coordinate makes the statement true, so the graph of \(x\gt 7\) is everything to the right of \(7\) and the graph of \(x\lt 7\) is everything to the left. An open circle means the boundary value is excluded and a filled circle means it is included. The graphs of \(x\gt 7\) and \(x\ge 7\) are the same ray apart from that one point, so the circle is the only difference between the two pictures.
The chain \(-5\lt 2x+3\le 17\) says both \(-5\lt 2x+3\) and \(2x+3\le 17\) at once, so its solutions graph as a single segment of the number line. Enter how many integers satisfy the chain.
hints: Work on all three parts at each step, the same way 8.3 solved a chain, and keep track of which end carries the strict symbol.

Subtracting \(3\) from all three parts gives \(-8\lt 2x\le 14\). Divide all three by the positive \(2\), then count the integers between the two ends, remembering that the end with the strict symbol is drawn open and is left out.
blocks.sol: Subtracting \(3\) from all three parts gives \(-8\lt 2x\le 14\), and dividing all three by the positive \(2\) gives \(-4\lt x\le 7\). The integers on the segment run from \(-3\) to \(7\), and \(7-(-3)+1=\boxed{11}\). The end at \(-4\) is drawn open, so \(-4\) is left out, while the end at \(7\) is drawn filled, so \(7\) is counted.

blocks.x: The point \((9,7)\) lies on the line \(y=3x-20\). Enter yes if \((9,7)\) is a solution of \(y\lt 3x-20\), and no if it is not.
hints: Substitute the point, putting \(9\) in for \(x\) and \(7\) in for \(y\), then check whether the resulting statement is true.
The point is on the line, so the two sides come out equal. The question is whether \(\lt\) is true when the two sides are equal.
blocks.sol: Substituting gives \(7\lt 3(9)-20\), which is \(7\lt 7\), false, so the answer is \(\boxed{\text{no}}\). A strict inequality is false wherever the two sides are equal, so no point of the line \(y=3x-20\) is a solution, just as an open circle on a number line means the endpoint is not included.

blocks.x: The graph of an inequality is the set of points that satisfy it. That is 7.2's definition of a graph with the equals sign replaced. A number is on the graph of \(x\le 3\) when substituting it makes the statement true, and a point \((x,y)\) is on the graph of \(y\gt 4x-1\) when substituting both coordinates makes it true. The one difference from an equation is how many points make it true. A linear equation in two letters is true only at the points of one line, so its graph is thin, while a linear inequality is true across whole areas, so its graph is a region.

blocks.cap: The two planes have the same boundary and the same side is shaded, so the dash is the only difference between them. The left boundary is dashed because its own points are not solutions and the right one is solid because they are. Below the rule the same distinction appears one dimension down, an open circle where the endpoint is left out and a filled circle where it is kept.

blocks.x: With one letter the boundary is a single point. With two letters it is the set of points where the two sides come out equal, the line \(y=mx+b\) that chapter 7 drew. Every other point of the plane sits on one side of it or the other, and two things are undecided, which side is the graph and whether the line belongs to it.

The line \(y=5x-14\) splits the plane into two sides, and \(y\gt 5x-14\) is true at every point of one side and false at every point of the other. The origin is not on that line, so substituting \((0,0)\) settles which side is which. Enter the word above or below for the side that holds the solutions.
hints: Substituting the origin puts \(0\) in for both letters, which leaves only the constant term on the right.

A true test means the origin is one of the solutions, so the side you want is the side the origin sits on. Put \(x=0\) into \(5x-14\) for the line's height there, then compare it with the origin's height of \(0\).
blocks.sol: Substituting \((0,0)\) gives \(0\gt -14\), which is true, so the origin is one of the solutions. At \(x=0\) the line is at \(y=-14\) while the origin is at \(y=0\), so the origin's side is the one \(\boxed{\text{above}}\). Testing one point settles the whole side, since the inequality is true at every point of one side and false at every point of the other.

blocks.x: The point \((12,16)\) lies on the line \(y=\frac{5}{3}x-4\), which is the boundary of \(y\ge \frac{5}{3}x-4\). A boundary is drawn dashed when its own points are not solutions and solid when they are. Decide whether \((12,16)\) is a solution, then enter the word, dashed or solid.
hints: The word depends on one yes or no question, whether the points of the boundary line are solutions. Substitute \((12,16)\), a point of that line, and see whether the inequality holds.
The right side at \(x=12\) is \(\frac{5}{3}(12)-4\), which is \(20-4\). Compare that with the point's \(y\)-coordinate of \(16\).
blocks.sol: The right side at \(x=12\) is \(\frac{5}{3}(12)-4=16\), the point's own \(y\)-coordinate, and \(16\ge 16\) is true, so \((12,16)\) is a solution and the boundary is drawn \(\boxed{\text{solid}}\). Every point of the line makes the two sides equal, so one check settles all of them. Under \(\gt\) and \(\lt\) equality is not allowed and the boundary is dashed, the number line's open and filled circles one dimension up.

blocks.x: The graph of \(y\gt mx+b\) is the half-plane above the line \(y=mx+b\). Take any point \((x_0,y_0)\) of that line, so \(y_0=mx_0+b\), and move straight up. The first coordinate is still \(x_0\), so the right side is still \(mx_0+b\), while the second coordinate is larger, so the statement is true there, and straight down it is false. Every point of the plane is above the line, below it, or on it, so every solution is above and none is below. The boundary is drawn dashed for a strict symbol and solid for \(\ge\) or \(\le\), which is the open and filled circle one dimension up.

The statement is true at every point of one side of the boundary and false at every point of the other, so substituting one point that is off the boundary settles the shaded side. The origin is the cheapest test, since substituting it puts zero in for both letters, and it works whenever the boundary line does not pass through it.
The boundary of \(y\gt \frac{3}{2}x\) is a line through the origin, so \((0,0)\) is not available as a test point. Enter the smallest integer \(y\) for which \((6,y)\) is a solution.
hints: Put \(x=6\) into the inequality. The right side becomes a single number, so what is left is an inequality in \(y\) alone.
That number is \(\frac{3}{2}(6)\), and the symbol is strict, so the boundary value itself is not a solution. The answer is the first integer above it.
blocks.sol: At \(x=6\) the inequality reads \(y\gt \frac{3}{2}(6)\), which is \(y\gt 9\), so the smallest integer is \(\boxed{10}\). The origin lies on the boundary and settles nothing, while \((6,10)\) lies off it and satisfies the inequality, so the shaded side is the one above the line.

blocks.x: Leonid Kantorovich was asked in the late 1930s to get the most out of a plywood factory's machines. He turned it into a question about the region of plans allowed by a list of inequalities, and linear programming began there.
The inequality \(3x-4y\gt 20\) is not solved for \(y\). Enter the largest integer \(y\) for which the point \((8,y)\) satisfies this inequality.
hints: Substituting \(x=8\) leaves an inequality in \(y\) alone. Check the sign of the coefficient of \(y\) before dividing, since 8.1's rule about dividing by a negative applies.
That inequality is \(24-4y\gt 20\), so \(-4y\gt -4\). Dividing both sides by \(-4\) reverses the direction.
blocks.sol: Substituting \(x=8\) gives \(24-4y\gt 20\), so \(-4y\gt -4\), and dividing by \(-4\) reverses the direction to \(y\lt 1\). The largest integer below \(1\) is \(\boxed{0}\). Checking, \(3(8)-4(0)=24\gt 20\), while \(3(8)-4(1)=20\) is not above \(20\). Keeping \(\gt\) through that division would give \(y\gt 1\), which has no largest integer at all.

blocks.x: An inequality written \(ax+by\le c\) can be graphed by either of two routes. One is to solve for \(y\) first, where 8.1's rule applies to the final division, so a negative \(b\) reverses the direction. Solving \(3x-4y\gt 20\) that way gives \(y\lt \frac{3x-20}{4}\), so the solutions are below the boundary even though the symbol is \(\gt\). The other route leaves the form alone. Draw \(ax+by=c\) from its intercepts the 7.5 way and test one point off it, shading its side if the test is true and the other side if it is false. Nothing is divided, so no direction reverses.

Several inequalities can hold at once, and a point is a solution only when it satisfies them all. Each has its own half-plane, and some have only one letter. The inequality \(x\ge k\) says nothing about \(y\), so its graph is every point on or right of the vertical line \(x=k\), and \(y\lt k\) graphs as everything below the horizontal line \(y=k\).
In the plane the graph of \(x\ge -6\) is a half-plane. Enter how many of the points \((-6,25)\), \(\left(-\frac{13}{2},0\right)\), \((3,-41)\), \((-7,-7)\) and \((-5,12)\) satisfy \(x\ge -6\).
hints: The inequality is a condition on \(x\) alone, so compare each first coordinate with \(-6\) and ignore the second one entirely.
Two of the five are close calls. One turns on whether \(\ge\) is true when the two sides are equal, and the other on how \(-\frac{13}{2}\) compares with \(-6\).
blocks.sol: Only the first coordinate matters. \(-6\ge -6\) is true, \(-\frac{13}{2}\ge -6\) is false, \(3\ge -6\) is true, \(-7\ge -6\) is false, and \(-5\ge -6\) is true, so the count is \(\boxed{3}\). The graph is the vertical line \(x=-6\) drawn solid together with everything to its right, and the second coordinate is free because \(y\) never appears in it.

blocks.x: A point is on the graph of two inequalities at once exactly when both substitutions come out true. Enter how many of \((3,4)\), \((4,7)\), \((5,4)\), \((6,5)\), \((2,1)\) and \((7,6)\) satisfy both \(y\lt 2x-1\) and \(x+y\ge 7\).
hints: Each inequality has its own half-plane, so every point needs two substitutions, and one false result is enough to leave it out.
Two of the points sit on a boundary. \((4,7)\) makes the first read \(7\lt 7\) and \((3,4)\) makes the second read \(7\ge 7\), and only one of those two symbols is true when the sides are equal.
blocks.sol: \((3,4)\), \((5,4)\), \((6,5)\) and \((7,6)\) satisfy both, so the count is \(\boxed{4}\). \((4,7)\) gives \(7\lt 7\), false, and \((2,1)\) gives \(3\ge 7\), false. Of the two points on a boundary, \((3,4)\) is included and \((4,7)\) is not, since \(x+y=7\) is drawn solid under \(\ge\) while \(y=2x-1\) is drawn dashed under \(\lt\).

blocks.x: The graph of several inequalities at once is the overlap of their half-planes. A point belongs when every substitution comes out true, so one false substitution is enough to leave it out. A corner of that region is a point where two of the boundary lines cross, and its coordinates come from solving those two boundary equations as a system, which is chapter 5's work and 7.6's picture. A crossing counts as a corner only when it also satisfies the inequalities that were not used to find it, and a crossing on a dashed boundary is at the edge of the region without being part of it.

The work is two moves per inequality. Draw the boundary, dashed for a strict symbol and solid otherwise, then test one point off it to decide which side is shaded. A region closed on every side contains finitely many points with integer coordinates, and those are counted one column at a time, fixing \(x\) and reading which \(y\) are allowed.

The points that satisfy all three of \(x\ge 1\), \(y\ge 2\) and \(3x+2y\le 20\) form a triangular region, and the edges are part of the region. Enter how many points with integer coordinates lie in that region.
hints: Count one vertical line at a time. Since \(y\ge 2\), every point in the region has \(3x\le 20-4=16\), so \(x\) is at most \(5\).
Set \(x=1\) in the third inequality to get \(2y\le 17\), so \(y\) is an integer from \(2\) to \(8\). Do the same at each \(x\) and add the counts.
blocks.sol: At \(x=1\) the third inequality becomes \(2y\le 17\), so \(y\) is an integer from \(2\) to \(8\) and that column has \(7\) points, and the same count at \(x=2,3,4,5\) is \(6\), \(4\), \(3\) and \(1\), with nothing left at \(x=6\), so the total is \(7+6+4+3+1=\boxed{21}\). At \(x=1\), \(x=3\) and \(x=5\) the bound on \(y\) is not a whole number, so the largest integer \(y\) is below it.

blocks.x: The points that satisfy \(3x+4y\le 26\), \(x-2y\ge -3\) and \(y\ge 0\) all at once form a triangular region. Two of its corners sit on the \(x\)-axis, and the third is where the boundary lines of the first two inequalities cross. Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of that third corner.
hints: The two boundary lines are \(3x+4y=26\) and \(x-2y=-3\), and the corner is the one point on both of them, so finding it is a chapter 5 system.
The second equation gives \(x=2y-3\). Substituting that into the first leaves an equation in \(y\) alone.
blocks.sol: The boundaries are \(3x+4y=26\) and \(x-2y=-3\). The second gives \(x=2y-3\), and substituting gives \(3(2y-3)+4y=26\), so \(10y-9=26\) and \(y=\boxed{\frac{7}{2}}\). The corner is \(\left(4,\frac{7}{2}\right)\), and \(y\ge 0\) holds there, so it really is a corner of the region.

blocks.x: Every region in this lesson was drawn and then read, for a count of the points inside it or for one corner. Nothing here asked which point of a region is the best one. Lesson 8.5, Optimization, asks exactly that, and the corners found here are the points to check.

review.x: The solutions of \(x-14\gt 9\) fill a ray on the number line, and the ray does not include the number it starts at. Enter that number.
hints: The starting number is the value that makes the two sides equal.
Adding \(14\) to both sides leaves the direction alone.
review.sol: Adding \(14\) to both sides leaves the direction alone and gives \(x\gt \boxed{23}\). At \(x=23\) the statement reads \(9\gt 9\), which is false, so the ray starts at \(23\) without including it.

review.x: Solve \(5x+7\le -13\). The solutions form a ray on the number line with a single circle at its endpoint. Enter one word, open or filled, for that circle.
hints: Subtract \(7\) from both sides, then divide both sides by \(5\). Both moves leave the direction of the sign alone, since \(5\) is positive.
Those moves give \(x\le -4\). Since the symbol is \(\le\) and not \(\lt\), check whether \(x=-4\) itself satisfies \(5x+7\le -13\).
review.sol: Subtracting \(7\) gives \(5x\le -20\), and dividing both sides by the positive \(5\) leaves the direction alone, so \(x\le -4\). At \(x=-4\) the left side is exactly \(-13\), and \(\le\) allows equality, so the circle is \(\boxed{\text{filled}}\). Everything to the left of \(-4\) is shaded, and \(-4\) is included in the solution set.

review.x: The solutions of \(-7\lt 3x+2\le 14\) form a segment with one end included and the other excluded. Enter the number at the excluded end.
hints: Do the same move to all three parts, then see which end carries the strict symbol.
Subtracting \(2\) from all three parts gives \(-9\lt 3x\le 12\), and dividing all three by the positive \(3\) leaves both directions as they are.
review.sol: Subtracting \(2\) gives \(-9\lt 3x\le 12\), and dividing by \(3\) gives \(-3\lt x\le 4\), so the excluded end is \(\boxed{-3}\). The strict symbol is at the lower end, so the open circle is at \(-3\) and the filled one is at \(4\).

review.x: Enter yes if \((6,-1)\) satisfies \(y\gt \frac{1}{3}x-5\), and no if it does not.
hints: Substitute \(6\) for \(x\) and \(-1\) for \(y\), then read whether the comparison is true.
The right side is \(\frac{1}{3}(6)-5\), which is \(2-5\).
review.sol: The right side is \(\frac{1}{3}(6)-5=-3\), and \(-1\gt -3\) is true, so the answer is \(\boxed{\text{yes}}\). On the number line \(-1\) sits to the right of \(-3\), which is what makes it the larger of the two.

review.x: The graph of \(y\lt 7x+2\) is a half-plane. Enter one word, dashed or solid, for how its boundary line is drawn.
hints: The boundary is the line where the two sides are equal, so check whether the inequality holds at those points.
At a point of the line the inequality reads as a number being strictly less than itself.
review.sol: At a point of \(y=7x+2\) the two sides are equal, and \(\lt\) is strict, so those points are not solutions and the line is drawn \(\boxed{\text{dashed}}\). A dashed boundary means its points are excluded, the same convention as an open circle on a number line.

review.x: Test the origin in \(y\le -4x+9\) to settle which side of the boundary line \(y=-4x+9\) holds the solutions. Enter the word above or below.
hints: Substituting \((0,0)\) turns the inequality into a statement with no variables in it, and whether that statement is true decides whether the origin is a solution.
The test comes out true, so the origin is a solution and its side is the one wanted. Put \(x=0\) into \(y=-4x+9\) and compare that height with the origin's height of \(0\).
review.sol: Substituting \((0,0)\) gives \(0\le 9\), which is true, so the origin is a solution. At \(x=0\) the origin is at \(y=0\) while the line is at \(y=9\), so the solutions lie \(\boxed{\text{below}}\). Checking the other side, \((0,20)\) gives \(20\le 9\), which is false.

review.x: The graph of \(y\lt 6\) in the plane is a half-plane. Enter how many of the seven points \((11,6)\), \((-2,5)\), \((0,-30)\), \(\left(4,\frac{13}{2}\right)\), \((7,-1)\), \((-9,0)\) and \((15,5)\) satisfy \(y\lt 6\).
hints: Only the second coordinate can matter here, since the inequality puts no condition on \(x\).
Write \(\frac{13}{2}\) as a decimal before comparing it with \(6\), and decide what the strict \(\lt\) does with a point whose second coordinate is exactly \(6\).
review.sol: Only the second coordinate matters, and the points with second coordinate below \(6\) are \((-2,5)\), \((0,-30)\), \((7,-1)\), \((-9,0)\) and \((15,5)\), so the count is \(\boxed{5}\). The other two fail because \(\frac{13}{2}=6.5\) is more than \(6\), and \((11,6)\) is on the boundary line, where the strict \(6\lt 6\) is false.

review.x: In the plane the graph of \(3x+4\lt 43\) is a half-plane whose boundary is a vertical line. Enter the \(x\)-coordinate that every point of that boundary has.
hints: Solve for \(x\) first. The result is a condition on \(x\) alone, so the boundary is vertical.
Subtracting \(4\) gives \(3x\lt 39\), and \(3\) is positive.
review.sol: Subtracting \(4\) gives \(3x\lt 39\), and dividing by the positive \(3\) gives \(x\lt \boxed{13}\). The shaded region is everything to the left of the line \(x=13\), and that line is drawn dashed, since the bound is strict.

review.x: The graph of \(6x+y\ge 5\) is a half-plane, and its boundary line is part of it. Enter the smallest integer \(y\) for which \((-2,y)\) lies in that half-plane.
hints: The first coordinate is the \(x\) value, so substituting \(x=-2\) into \(6x+y\ge 5\) leaves an inequality in \(y\) only.
That gives \(-12+y\ge 5\), and adding \(12\) to both sides leaves the direction alone.
review.sol: Substituting \(x=-2\) gives \(-12+y\ge 5\), so \(y\ge 17\) and the smallest integer available is \(\boxed{17}\). The inequality is not strict, so \(17\) itself counts. Checking, \(6(-2)+17=5\), and \(5\ge 5\) is true.

review.x: The graph of \(2x+3y\le 31\) is a half-plane. Enter the largest integer \(y\) for which the point \((5,y)\) lies in it.
hints: Substitute \(x=5\) and solve what is left for \(y\).
That gives \(3y\le 21\), and \(3\) is positive, so dividing by it leaves the direction alone.
review.sol: Substituting gives \(10+3y\le 31\), so \(3y\le 21\) and \(y\le \boxed{7}\). Checking, \(2(5)+3(7)=31\), and \(31\le 31\) is true, so \(7\) is allowed.

review.x: Enter the smallest integer \(y\) for which the point \((3,y)\) satisfies \(4x-5y\le -28\).
hints: Substituting \(x=3\) leaves an inequality in \(y\) with a negative coefficient.
That gives \(-5y\le -40\), and dividing both sides by \(-5\) reverses the direction.
review.sol: Substituting \(x=3\) gives \(12-5y\le -28\), so \(-5y\le -40\), and dividing by \(-5\) reverses the direction to \(y\ge \boxed{8}\). At \(y=8\) the left side is \(12-40=-28\), and a \(\le\) statement is true when the two sides are equal, so \(8\) itself works, while \(y=7\) gives \(-23\), which is greater than \(-28\).

review.x: The origin lies on the boundary line of \(y\gt \frac{5}{4}x\), so a test point has to come from somewhere off that line. Enter the smallest integer \(y\) for which \((20,y)\) is a solution.
hints: Substituting \(x=20\) turns the right side into a single number.
That number is \(\frac{5}{4}(20)=25\), and the symbol is strict, so \(25\) is not allowed.
review.sol: At \(x=20\) the inequality reads \(y\gt 25\), so the smallest integer is \(\boxed{26}\). The point \((20,26)\) is then a usable test point, and it sits above the line, so the graph is the region above.

review.x: Enter how many of the six points \((0,0)\), \((1,6)\), \((5,1)\), \((3,5)\), \((2,1)\) and \((4,0)\) satisfy both \(y\le x+2\) and \(x+y\gt 4\).
hints: Substitute each point into \(y\le x+2\) first and then into \(x+y\gt 4\), and count only the points where both come out true.
Two of the six sit exactly on a boundary, \((3,5)\) on \(y=x+2\) and \((4,0)\) on \(x+y=4\), so settle each of those by whether that inequality is strict.
review.sol: \((5,1)\) gives \(1\le 7\) and \(6\gt 4\), and \((3,5)\) gives \(5\le 5\) and \(8\gt 4\), so both pass. \((1,6)\) fails the first, and \((0,0)\), \((2,1)\) and \((4,0)\) fail the second, so the count is \(\boxed{2}\). The two boundary cases come out differently because \(\le\) includes its boundary line, drawn solid, while \(\gt\) excludes its own, drawn dashed.

review.x: The boundary lines of \(x+y\le 20\) and \(x-y\ge 4\) cross at one point. Enter the \(x\)-coordinate of that point.
hints: The crossing is the one point lying on both boundary lines, so it satisfies \(x+y=20\) and \(x-y=4\) at once, the kind of system chapter 5 solved.
Adding the two equations removes \(y\), since one carries \(+y\) and the other \(-y\).
review.sol: Adding \(x+y=20\) and \(x-y=4\) gives \(2x=24\), so \(x=\boxed{12}\). The crossing is \((12,8)\), and both inequalities hold there with equality, so it is a corner of the region they share.

review.x: Enter how many points with integer coordinates satisfy all three of \(x\ge 0\), \(y\ge 0\) and \(2x+y\le 6\).
hints: Count one vertical line at a time. Since \(y\) is at least \(0\), the sum \(2x+y\) is never below \(2x\), so \(2x\le 6\) and \(x\) runs only from \(0\) to \(3\).
At \(x=0\) the third inequality reads \(y\le 6\), so there are seven values of \(y\), and each step right lowers the cap by \(2\).
review.sol: At \(x=0\) the allowed \(y\) run from \(0\) to \(6\), which is \(7\) points, then \(5\) at \(x=1\), \(3\) at \(x=2\) and \(1\) at \(x=3\), so the count is \(7+5+3+1=\boxed{16}\). All three inequalities are non-strict, so the points on all three edges are counted.

review.x: The inequality \(6x-3y\lt 12\) is graphed in the plane. Enter the word, above or below, for the side of its boundary line where the solutions lie.
hints: Get \(y\) by itself in \(6x-3y\lt 12\). The step that divides by the coefficient of \(y\) is the one to watch.
A test point settles it with no algebra at all. Check whether the origin satisfies \(6x-3y\lt 12\), then put \(x=0\) into \(6x-3y=12\) to see where the boundary sits at that same \(x\).
review.sol: Subtracting \(6x\) gives \(-3y\lt 12-6x\), and dividing by \(-3\) reverses the direction to \(y\gt 2x-4\), so the solutions lie \(\boxed{\text{above}}\). Testing the origin gives the true statement \(0\lt 12\), and the origin sits above \(y=2x-4\), which crosses the \(y\)-axis at \(-4\).

review.x: The boundary lines of \(3x-2y\ge -4\) and \(x+2y\le 16\) cross at a corner of the region where both hold. Enter the \(y\)-coordinate of that corner.
hints: The corner is the point on both lines \(3x-2y=-4\) and \(x+2y=16\), so solve them as a system.
Adding the two equations removes \(y\) at once, since one carries \(-2y\) and the other \(+2y\).
review.sol: Adding \(3x-2y=-4\) and \(x+2y=16\) gives \(4x=12\), so \(x=3\), and \(3+2y=16\) gives \(y=\boxed{\frac{13}{2}}\). Both \(\ge\) and \(\le\) allow equality, so their boundary lines are solid and the corner \(\left(3,\frac{13}{2}\right)\) is itself in the region.
